In a theoretical model, a collection of dipoles with permanent moments is examined, situated between two optical elements, where some dipoles interact with an incoming optical field while others do not. It is shown that, under certain conditions, these dipoles can form long-lived pairs in a bosonic state, similar to parametric down-conversion in standard optical systems. A specific change occurs in the system's equivalent cavity length when this pair generation is considered. It is also proposed that this model can be used to produce optical squeezed states through a process called parametric amplification, resulting from this pair generation.

This study introduces a complete configuration interaction approach to examine the magnetic properties of a pair of exchange-coupled electron valleys in silicon. Employing a set of four valley effective mass Hamiltonians, we theoretically investigate multiple spin states and current distribution patterns. Our calculations show that the interaction between the two electron valleys' exchange forces can be understood through the concept of effective two-level systems and that certain current distributions arise due to inter-valley scattering effects. In particular, we find that a particular arrangement of two electrons, known as the collinear geometry, produces the strongest exchange interaction and that our model accurately predicts observed currents in actual experiments. However, it also reveals that, in certain non-collinear configurations, additional distant points contribute significantly to the observed currents and that our model may underestimate the currents in these cases. Overall, these results provide valuable insights into the complex behavior of exchange interaction and currents in exchange-coupled electron valleys and highlight the importance of carefully considering spin-orbit coupling and multi-valley effects in interpreting data from actual experiments.

Researchers investigated the electrical properties of mercury-telluride materials with decreasing thickness, down to a critical point where a quantum well forms and exhibits no energy gap. Experimental data from transport measurements and theoretical calculations from tight-binding models both show that conduction occurs along specific paths defined by particle-hole symmetry, influenced by the helical movement of particles and the conservation of angular momentum. Notably, this phenomenon persists despite the unique scattering properties of Majorana bound states present at these quantum well interfaces.

Nominal multi-user access (OAM) is a suitable solution for providing high data rates to vehicles in urban areas, and by incorporating it into a cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMa) protocol, a single base station can serve multiple vehicles, and in doing so, reduce latency and improve reliability. Through the use of layered decoding in NOMa, road safety sensors can assist in avoiding collisions without compromising road safety. A novel cooperative NOMa protocol is proposed for a four-road junction, and its performance is analyzed using Markov chain models. The protocol's benefits are evident when compared to traditional orthogonal multiple access (OMA) protocols, and in doing so, it offers higher reliability and lower latency for vehicles in urban environments.

In Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD), uplink and downlink portions of a cell can be adjusted in real-time to meet changing traffic demands. This paper tackles the optimal scheduling of TDD configurations in a multi-cell environment by schedulable base stations that operate in an uplink-focused or downlink-focused mode. We've developed a novel, non-cooperative game called the Schedulable Base Station Game (SBSG), where the players aim to maximize their downlink throughput. We've also developed an optimal solution to the SSG using a concept called a Correlated Equilibrium (CE). By utilizing a game-theoretic approach, our solution can be computed efficiently using an algorithm called fictitious play. Numerical results show that our solution leads to an outcome near-optimal and provides network-wide benefits.

Although earlier research suggested that a particular type of Hall anomaly observed in BSCCO could result from a combination of lattice friction and vacancy movement, the precise cause remained unclear. This study analyzes the vacancy drift component of the Hall anomaly using the Nernst-Ettingshausen effect and finds that the vacancy movement can account for the entire anomaly, as evidenced by the observed Peltumn anomaly and specific heat shift at the anomaly peak. Furthermore, our analysis of the BSCCO data reveals that the average distance that vacancies move is approximately 10 times larger than a single lattice vortex.

In the three-dimensional Ising universality class, we have identified a new conformal field theory-related parameter through the ratio of two specific moment ratios, denoted as R_sub_2 and R_sub_3, which correspond to moments of the singular specific heat. Our analysis indicates that at a critical temperature, these moment ratios remain constant, a finding that is consistent with the constancy of all moment ratios observed in previous studies. This result is in line with the expected behavior of moments in the three-dimensional Ising universality class.

This research confirms a long-standing hypothesis by Izumi regarding characterizing the subfactors of finite index, in terms of a finite-dimensional commuting square of categories. Specifically, we have characterized a category of unitary braided symmetric monoidal type as generating a subfactor of finite depth, by examining its underlying abelian category. Additionally, in terms of this abelian category, we have characterized another key property – the 3-dimensional index.

Recent advancements in science-driven machine learning, specifically in solving complex physical systems through the application of known physical laws, have highlighted the potential of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs). By encoding conservation laws into a data-driven model, researchers have been able to solve various scientific and engineering problems with lower data requirements and long-term stability. This paper presents a novel approach by reinterpreting HNNs as autoencoders that use physical loss functions in their reconstruction, which not only facilitates straightforward hyperparameter optimization via denoising autoencoder loss but also paves the way for developing improved Hamiltonian systems by leveraging Hamiltonian HNNs to train vector field components as descriptive basis functions.

The growing popularity of machine learning systems has sparked concerns about user confidence in their safety and reliability, prompting research into user-centric assessments of algorithmic reliability. This paper proposes a novel approach, where a human works alongside multiple machine learning agents in a repeated game, task, or simulation. Human partners are assigned numerical values reflecting their perceived reliability, which can influence how they choose to collaborate with the algorithm. These trust metrics, along with the discovery that human feedback can be used to identify and rectify inaccuracies in the data, can enhance the reliability of the algorithm's evaluation.

In security inspections, identifying prohibited items from luggage is essential for preventing threats at critical infrastructure facilities like airports. While previous studies in this field have primarily focused on theoretical aspects, real-world applications face significant challenges due to the vast number of potential prohibited items and the need for safety and efficiency. In response, we created a high-quality dataset containing over one million images with more than 10,000 different prohibited items, covering a wide range of objects commonly found in luggage. We also introduced a novel Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM) to enhance the performance of prohibited items detection models by enabling them to learn simultaneously from positive and negative examples. Experimental results demonstrate that our Lateral Inhibition Model outperforms existing methods on our new benchmark, setting a new standard for prohibited items detection in security inspections.

We introduce a new invariant for links in $T^2 \times I$ that is robust under the equivalence of twisted conjugacy. This invariant fulfills the robust computation criteria under the addition of robust generators under volume hypothesis. As an outcome, many links in $T^2 \times I$ can be computed accurately using their simplified forms derived from their twisted conjugacy classes.

The primary factor influencing word sense disambiguation (WSD) performance is context, but existing context vectors constructed from semantic representations like Word2Vec often fail to capture comprehensive context information. This limitation stems from their reliance on co-occurrence statistics, which can be a sparse indicator of context. To address this issue, we propose a context vector augmentation technique for WSD, integrating additional linguistic knowledge from context sentences through a data-driven gloss construction method and a context vector learning method. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets for English and Chinese demonstrate that this proposed approach significantly enhances traditional WSD models by a notable margin, achieving an average performance boost of 6.11% and 3.61%, respectively.

This study defines a novel approach to representing the reciprocal Gamma function through a specific form of the zeta function, denoted as $\mathcal{Z}(s)$, and later an modified version, $\mathcal{R}\mathcal{Z}(s)$, which excludes the pole at $s=1$. Two new integral formulas, including one starting from $s=0$, are established for $\mathcal{Z}(s)$ and $\mathcal{R}\mathcal{Z}(s)$, thereby proving the feasibility of the previously mentioned expressions. Furthermore, these developments enable the representation of the reciprocal Gamma function via $\mathcal{R}\mathcal{Z}(s)$, offering useful implications for the derivation of the Gautschi inequality and the related inequalities of the Gamma function.

The LHC's unique proton-nucleus beam setup provides an opportunity to produce rare particles like the Higgs boson through more powerful processes. However, the top quark is already a relatively light particle, making certain proton-proton processes sufficient for a dedicated top quark search. When the LHC operated at 7 TeV in 2010, we utilized the LHCb detector to analyze proton-lead data at 7 TeV and found a small excess of top quark events in a region where the top quark was almost impossible to find in proton-proton collisions. This analysis demonstrated the potential for discovering new particles by comparing the results to a theoretical prediction of 0.056 top quark events, based on the more powerful processes.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL task, which converts natural language descriptions of queries into actual SQL statements that can be executed on databases. Our method innovatively adopts a end-to-end neural network architecture, which is capable of interpreting natural language and generating SQL statements across different database schemas. Notably, our model employs a neural auxiliary task that facilitates learning from examples of single-column entity extraction, utilizing both structural and linguistic information from the data. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency compared to existing baseline models.

This paper delves into the application of differential privacy to graph data and explores various DPs techniques tailored to graph analytics and learning. We outline key challenges in incorporating differential privacy into graph-based learning and provide an overview of DP methods that preserve dependencies within network data. As the field of DP on graph data is still emerging, our research on DP for network learning and analytics is classified into four categories: node property learning, graph topology learning and analytics, combined learning and analytics, and hybrid models of node, topology, and attribute learning. Our work also encompasses a comprehensive examination of prior DP studies on network learning and learning and can serve as a resource for future investigations in this area.

The Euclid telescope and satellite have been in development for over two decades, building on the legacy of previous experiments like Euclid's forerunners, the Euclid heritage science. These investigations have been in full swing for a long time, often using the same celestial objects and methodologies as Euclid will in the coming years. Given the significant investment in the Euclid endeavor, it's important to acknowledge and celebrate the heritage science achievements. This paper summarizes the main scientific endeavors of the Euclid heritage science and the heritage instrumentation, with a focus on space-based instruments. The main accomplishments of these investigations are also highlighted.

In this research, a novel approach to generating complex road networks for testing the Advanced Lane Keeping System (ALKS) is introduced. Although ALKs, which detects and maintains the vehicle's position on a marked road, has been developed to prevent accidents, its limitation to simple road conditions poses a significant safety concern. Currently, only basic road patterns like gentle curves and consistent line roads are considered valid for ALKs, enabling the system to simply follow the road's path. However, an accident can still occur due to the system's inability to account for sudden changes in road geometry. As a result, the accident prevention function of ALKs is compromised. To address this issue, the proposed method involves creating challenging road networks by combining a value-added algorithm that checks the accessibility of generated paths and an automatic creation system based on complex, interlocking Bezier curves. This allows for the efficient generation of complex road networks that can effectively test the limitations of the ALKs system.

Music recommendation systems should not only suggest new tunes but also communicate the music's mood, style, and genre in a narrative form. This capability would empower listeners to comprehend the underlying patterns in their favorite playlists, thereby improving the overall music recommendation experience. However, the task of automatically creating descriptive music narratives using language remains an underexplored area of research. To address this challenge, we propose a new evaluation metric that assesses the ability of algorithms to generate engaging and accurate descriptions of music playlists. We believe that developing such narrative capabilities is crucial for advancing the overall music recommendation experience and encouraging researchers to explore this uncharted territory.

Quantum hydrodynamics can be understood through a stochastic framework by applying appropriate transformations to the Gross-Pitaevskii mean-field equation and its conjugate. This approach yields a set of random phase-space trajectories that mimic the dynamics of interacting bosons. Notably, these quantum hydrodynamic equations derive from modified versions of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation where the interaction term is replaced with a cubic, density-based energy term. As a result, we can solve for quantum hydrodynamic trajectories and obtain precise solutions for density and flow velocity profiles following sudden changes in trap conditions. This methodology provides an efficient and accurate means of modeling quantum many-body systems consisting of interacting bosons.

Temporal action detection is a specialized task within the realm of video action understanding, focused on pinpointing the start and end of actions in video content. Current top approaches usually process the video content in a frame-by-frame sequence, neglecting the contextual connections between adjacent frames. This context can be particularly useful in identifying actions, as they are often closely related to the surrounding non-action events. To address this, we introduce a novel context aggregation network, which is designed to integrate temporal contexts around the action boundaries. This context includes both the previous and subsequent events that occur before and after the action. By aggregating these temporal contexts, we can enhance the performance of temporal action detection. Furthermore, to prevent the model from being negatively affected by the non-action events, we introduce a dual context aggregation strategy that balances the context aggregation with the classification performance. This strategy allows the network to focus on the most relevant parts of the temporal context, thereby improving the overall accuracy of the action detection.

A peculiar phenomenon observed in the JET tokamak during recent deuterium operations is the emergence of low-frequency, leaf-shaped magnetic fluctuations known as Palm Tree Modes (PTMs). These modes significantly impact confined particles and lead to broadened energy transitions at the plasma edge. PTMs are typically found in high-density discharges with strong leaf modes but persist even in scenarios with moderate density. They exhibit distinct characteristics, such as a specific rotation direction, localized impact on lateral channels, and the absence of extensive energy transitions. This suggests that PTMs are not primarily caused by a single global mechanism. Instead, they may be influenced by a discharge's specific rotation properties and perhaps a different driving force. This study seeks to identify common features of PTMs and explore the factors that may be crucial for their development, including rotation properties and the role of other parameters, such as the ELM mode in driving PTM development.

This research addresses the challenge of collision avoidance in mobile robots within a collaborative multi-robot environment, where robots navigate simultaneously to shared target locations. A novel field concept, the dynamic vortex potential, is introduced and shown to effectively guide robots towards their desired points while evading both stationary obstacles and other obstacles within a flexible framework. The properties of the dynamic vortex potential are explored, and its application in providing smooth path planning for mobile robots is demonstrated through experimental validation.

This study examines the rare occurrences of an uncommon symbol within a generated sequence of symbols, where the probability of an uncommon symbol appearing in position $n$ is influenced by the preceding symbol from the previous position, and is based on a pre-established system. Under a specific condition, we examine the exponential rate at which large deviations from a rare symbol occur and investigate its relationship with a corresponding system known as a dual system. Additionally, we explore how this exponential rate is affected by another form of deviation, which considers deviations from a rare double sequence, and is related to its corresponding dual system.

Proposed in this paper is a novel application of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IIS) in radar systems, where surfaces control the flow of radar signals by adjusting surface-controlled elements (SCEs). By utilizing IIS, the quality of the main radar path can be significantly improved, allowing for more accurate target parameter estimation through methods such as maximum likelihood estimation. Simulations using realistic scenarios with publicly available data demonstrate that even with limited radar power, the addition of IIS can substantially improve the accuracy of target parameter estimation, particularly when the direct radar path is weak or obstructed. The results also indicate that the IRS-assisted radar system can achieve comparable performance to a power-intensive radar system with a strong direct path.

High-performance fuzzers can automatically find vulnerabilities in software by combining test inputs in innovative ways. Despite their effectiveness, there is limited information on how to enhance or contrast their performance. This study explores the effects of contrast fuzzing on a range of performance metrics, including bug discovery, crash diversity, and program coverage, when different fuzzers are pitted against each other. By evaluating 15 fuzzers across 14 target programs, this study provides a foundation for future researchers in understanding fuzzer performance and designing effective fuzzing strategies.

The prevailing trend in continual learning research is to enhance pre-trained models that transfer knowledge from source domains to target domains. We examine whether this paradigm is optimal by introducing a new continuous learning setting, where the training process is unbroken and model updates follow one another. We observe that under this setting, the order of training significantly impacts final performance on the last task, but surprisingly, simple baselines achieve high accuracy without the need for elaborate strategies like curriculum learning or replaying old data. In fact, these results indicate that a simple linear combination of pre-trained models can capture complex patterns of continuous data, challenging the current approach of using pre-trained models in continuous learning settings.

Given a metric space X, a real number p greater than or equal to 1, and a region γ in a specific homotopy class within X, we identify a surface w in the same homotopy class as γ that has the minimal norm among all variations in that homotopy class. Notably, this minimal surface w is independent of the choice of homotopy class γ. Furthermore, a corresponding variation of this proves useful in the development of a quasi-flat family in a larger metric space.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions to the generic parabolic initial boundary value problems on the real line. This specific volume focuses on cases where the initial data is not stationary, but instead, has an exponential decay rate. At one end of the real line, the initial data converges to an unstable stationary solution, while at the opposite end, it decays exponentially fast. Solutions to such problems typically exhibit distinct long-term behaviors, either decaying exponentially, algebraically, or following a hybrid time decay pattern. This particular line of research was not covered in the first two volumes of our work. It is important to note that this research was conducted with respect to the standard $L^\infty$ norm.

Recent experiments using gamma-gamma array have discovered multiple low-lying excited states in 64Ni, and theoretical calculations with random quantum interactions combined with experimental data have revealed that a zero-spin, 2+2 state can be formed by a shape mixture of two different quadrupole shapes. A new study employing two-component Interacting Boson Model and shell model in the Gaussian Spacing and Drude models investigates the quadrupole characteristics of 2+2 zero-spin states in an iron to nickel isotopic chain, and finds evidence that a strong quadrupole mixture exists in 64Ni, whereas in 62,60Fe, the quadrupole characteristics are predominantly exhibited by two distinct excited 2+2 states. Furthermore, a new iron to nickel spin system has been analyzed in terms of quadrupole-quadrupole Hamiltonian and two distinct quadrupole shapes have been identified in 64Ni at zero-spin 2+4 and 2+44 energy levels with similar quadrupole alignment energies.

The concept of L- Lipschitz games was originally proposed by Daskalakis, Papadimitriou, and Ruess to examine how the existence and stability of approximate equilibria, such as $\epsilon$- Nash equilibria, are affected by small changes in query complexity. Since its introduction, several classes of Lipschitz games have been developed, each demonstrating the feasibility of efficient algorithms for finding approximate equilibria. However, the ability of these algorithms to remain robust to more complicated forms of query complexity sensitivity had not been thoroughly investigated. To address this gap, we established lower bounds for the query complexity of finding Lipschitz equilibria in a broader range of game types, specifically in (k,q)- games where the likelihood of a player receiving an L- Lipschitz payoff is denoted by k, and the games were analyzed under different values of q. Our findings indicate that for quadratic games (where (2,1)- games are equivalent to quadratic games), the complexity of finding an equilibrium is at least O(klog(k)q+1), and for cubic games (where (3,1)- games represent cubic games), the complexity is at least $\Omega(k^{0.757}q+1)$. These lower bounds are of particular interest given recent algorithmic advancements in finding equilibria in (k,q)- games, and our results are considered near-optimal in terms of how they scale with respect to K and Q.

Machine learning model performance assessment is often done through task-specific evaluation metrics, typically calculated over a test set that the model hasn't seen before. In instance-based learning models, an additional step involves hyperparameter tuning to optimize a model's assessment performance. A frequent strategy for tuning hyperparameters is employing k-fold cross-validation to create an average performance estimate over multiple model iterations. Nevertheless, the variability in this estimate can be considerable, potentially undermining the reliability of hyperparameter selection. This study investigates an enhanced cross-validation technique called J-K fold validation to reduce standard deviation and increase the consistency in parameter efficacy evaluation. Our experiments, carried out on various natural language processing models and datasets, indicate that J-K fold validation yields a considerably lower standard deviation in evaluation metrics compared to its conventional counterpart. As a result, it is likely to lead to more optimal parameter selection when paired with objective functions that consider evaluation metric distribution.

Recently, Network-Network Minimization (NNM)-based strategies have been Now widely used in various knowledge learning tasks, resulting in the development of various models designed to fulfill particular application requirements. These models include the Single-Student Architecture (SSA), which is the most extensively studied design, and several innovative concepts such as the Multi-Teacher Architecture (MRA) and the Circular Architecture (CNN). This paper provides a thorough examination of NNM-based models from beginning to end, beginning with an in-depth analysis of their working principles and NNM mechanisms, as well as their performance enhancements achieved through the use of innovative designs and application to a diverse range of tasks including multi-view classification, semi-supervised classification, and graph classification. This examination will guide researchers in developing more effective models by identifying suitable models for specific tasks and understanding how to optimize NNM mechanisms to improve their performance.

We introduce a streamlined algebraic framework that utilizes exponential, logarithmic, and algebraic operations to enhance the efficiency of the exact maximum a posteriori probability calculation in graphical models, following the principles of linear programming and tree-structured variable dependencies. This improvement builds upon the work of De and Kaskoki (2019) and significantly accelerates the computation by a factor of O(log n) per update, where n is the total number of possible state combinations for the graph variables. This enhancement is particularly beneficial for large-state graphs, and we demonstrate the practical application of our method in a constrained optimization context, enabling real-time control of complex robotic systems.

Our research employs a single laser technique to study the effects of photon recoil in an ultra-cold Sr gas at temperatures below 1 microKelvin. We demonstrate that, due to the photons' momentum, the atomic resonance appears to be split into two distinct peaks, and that as the laser's intensity increases, even in the saturated regime, the resonance peaks maintain their characteristic 'V' shape. Furthermore, by analyzing how an absorption signal varies with laser detuning in a non-saturated regime, we are able to precisely determine the recoil frequency, and in turn, calculate the photons' momentum, which aligns with predictions made by established theory.

When subjected to high stress rates, loose suspenses undergo shear thickening, shifting from their initial low friction state to a high friction state. This study analyzes a broad range of experiments on shear thickening transitions, sourcing data from publications that varied in their presentation styles, symbols, and formatting. By plotting these datasets against universal coordinates, researchers discovered that they converge to distinct curves that represent the transition's critical properties, in line with modern understanding of nonequilibrium systems. Notably, the onset of the high friction state can be described by a single order parameter, while the stress and strain rate exhibit power law relationships with specific exponents. Suspensions with different particle sizes, concentrations, and material properties demonstrate the generality of this approach in characterizing the complex behavior of shear thickening transitions.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$, which is derived from the universal R-matrix of the quantum group $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$. This paper focuses on the subalgebra $R(n)_0$ of $R(n)$ consisting of elements that commute with $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n$, and demonstrates that $R(n)_0$ is isomorphic to the centralizer Zassenhaus algebra $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ first identified by Cherednik. A connection between the algebra $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the quantum group $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$ is then established, and the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be classified by a family of Gelfand-Tsetlin graphs. These graphs were previously associated with the classical limit of $U(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$ through Macdonald polynomials, and a link between the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the Gelfand-Tsetlin graphs is further demonstrated. This connection leads to the computation of the Hilbert-Poincaré series of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, and a formula for its quantum dimension is obtained.

Our study reveals that in a bilayer honeycomb magnetic structure with triplons, twisted superfluid and supersolid phases can emerge in the presence of strong interlayer interactions, Dzyaloshinskii-Molodowsky forces, and an external magnetic field. A supersolid state arises from the crystal formation of twisted superfluid in one dimension, and can also be produced by an interplay of external magnetic field and interlayer interactions without the need for intralayer DMI. Notably, our study also shows that an Luttinger liquid state can be realized from a twisted supersolid in certain parameter ranges. Additionally, we found that an external magnetic field can induce a transition from a twisted supersolid to a twisted Luttinger liquid. An in-depth analysis of the system's properties in the twisted Luttinger liquid state is also provided.

This study examines WIMP-nucleus collisions in detail, focusing on how their three-dimensional behavior can influence the design of direct detection experiments. Specifically, we analyze the correlation between the incident velocity and recoil angle of colliding pairs in three dimensions. Our findings reveal that, for neutralinos and certain supersymmetric quarkless particles like gravitinos and goldstinos scattering off various target nuclei, a distinct pattern emerges where the recoil angle sharply decreases as the incident WIMP-nucleos's speed increases within the effective scattering range. Additionally, our research indicates that three-dimensional simulations of scattering events result in notable alterations to the energy distribution when observed from different angles, with this effect being more pronounced at lower recoil angles. These simulated 3-D simulations also yield energy spectrum modification factors of approximately 1.5-2.5 compared to their one-dimensional counterparts. Notably, this three-dimensional nature of WIMP scattering may have significant implications for the accuracy of current and future direct detection experiments, with especially sensitive low-threshold experiments like Super-Kamiokande's COHERENS may be affected.

This is when personalisation yields positive, neutral, or negative effects, resulting in users either gaining access to relevant information, regular search outcomes, or missing relevant posts. We are considering the advantages of a new type of particle collider with cross-colliding 1-10 TeV muons and 1-10 TeV scale magnetic fields. This design, called a muon-particle collider (MPC), is distinct from conventional proposals for high-energy muon colliders. An MPC would be a revolutionary facility for studying the Higgs boson and potentially discovering new particles, like those related to the muon-particle collider's energy scale, the electroweak scale, and possibly the top quark. It is also an outstanding platform for studying forward scattering and a wide range of other phenomena. This design is a highly versatile and adaptable facility. We will outline the scientific potential of a 14 TeV muon-proton collider with a 10 TeV muon and a 2.5 TeV proton, along with alternative modes of operation, such as a 10 TeV muon and an 8 TeV proton, and Drell-Yan runs. This proposal is complemented by analyses conducted with state-of-the-art simulation tools like GENIE, MiNIA, MadGraph, MadSpin, Whizard, and recola.

A novel approach to generating four-dimensional MRI scans utilizing motion-corrected two-dimensional images is presented. This technique builds upon a previously developed method for creating three-dimensional MRI scans from sequential two-dimensional scans, taking into account movement in multiple directions. Accompling this motion correction across more than three sequential scans poses significant technical challenges. To overcome these challenges, the scan resolution was adjusted and the gradient strength was adjusted to facilitate diffusionless small-area motion. A novel, adjustable coil combination strategy was also developed to account for variable coil positioning due to scanning. As a result, high-resolution, fully three-dimensional MRI scans were successfully obtained free-breathing individuals without respiratory monitoring using a turbo spin-echo MRI sequence. Two trials were conducted to validate the scanning method, producing scans with a resolution of 0.6 millimeters per cubic millimeter in two different phantom scenarios. These scans demonstrated minimal geometric distortion and a high level of contrast, with contrast-to-noise and signal-to-noise ratios of 3.1 and 60.1, respectively.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to designing controllers that can safeguard a class of nonlinear systems against malicious actions by an external agent. The focus is on ensuring that desired behaviors are maintained by a predefined set of functions known as control barrier functions, which are subject to input limitations. The method proposed is rooted in geometric principles and results in a controller with an order no greater than that of the smallest Lie derivative containing a non-zero constant. If specific conditions are satisfied, the paper develops an alternative, parameterized definition of safety and derives a novel, exponentially stable barrier function that adheres to specific conditions. Leveraging this development, the proposed approach is able to achieve secure control synthesis under certain conditions, as well as in cases where the systems dynamics exhibit Brockett's property. Furthermore, the research aims to reduce the reliance on high-order constant Lie derivatives, resulting in more practical applications.

In rough set theory, representing knowledge fragments like concepts and rules within regions is a key application. This paper builds on previous work by expressing simple first-order logic formulae as an extended CF-approximation space, also known as an approximation table. By doing so, various region types, including concepts and rules, can be depicted as different subsets of these enhanced CF-approximation spaces.

The paired-permutation test, a well-established statistical test, is known to suffer from simulation errors when dealing with high-dimensional data due to an increasing number of comparisons. Our research aims to mitigate this issue by demonstrating that numerical inaccuracies can be significantly reduced, particularly in paired settings, through the use of von Neumann's up-down sequence and an efficient algorithm for calculating permutations. These methods are easily adaptable to existing software and can process a substantial number of permutations in a short amount of time. Our study also showcases the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the BrainScope device for diagnosing concussions, the KDD Cup 2016 challenge for early sepsis detection, and the UCI Machine Learning Repository for credit card fraud prevention.

Researchers face significant challenges in obtaining comprehensive and reliable data for container shipping sector studies due to the scarcity of unified datasets spanning long periods. A new all-encompassing container shipping sector dataset has been created to overcome these data limitations, covering container shipping freight rates, vessel market prices, shipping statistics, and scrap fees from 1966 to 2019. The dataset includes monthly data on freight rates, shipping quantities, and various vessel market prices, as well as annual data on container prices. Its consistency has been demonstrated through comparison with prominent industry reports and academic studies, and its utility has been proved through replicating established shipping index series and producing previously unpublished findings.

We define a new concept called veering triangulations within the context of closed surfaces, identifying them as a distinct subset of oriented veering graphs associated with trivalent surfaces. Following this definition, we demonstrate that veering triangulations possess an index of one under the veering graphs action of the surface group, allowing us to obtain the surface subgroup of the braid group as a fibered subgroup. This approach provides an alternative method for obtaining previous results by Hatcher and Margalit, and Guirardel and Levitt, who utilized more complex graphs to achieve similar outcomes.

Graph neural networks have been successfully applied to analyze complex systems, yet their intricate designs often hindered comprehension. As LSODI applications grow in prominence, there is a pressing need for clear and actionable insights from GNN models. While prior methods have achieved graph simplification through techniques like vertex contraction and edge removal, they failed to produce a directed graph that maintains the efficiency of the original model. This research introduces a novel approach, the Learned Sparsification framework for Interpretable Graph Neural Networks, which achieves undirected graph simplification by modifying both the architecture and input to the model. Our method leverages a pruned subgraph model that selectively emphasizes a subset of nodes and edges, and we further enhance the interpretability by allowing node and edge connectivity to be integrated into the model's decision-making process. Experimental results on seven diverse GNN tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods in both performance and interpretability, and we also show that the pruned subgraphs align with human domain knowledge and underlying data distributions.

The CountSketch algorithm, a basic and highly efficient method for approximate frequent item identification, is known to produce incorrect ID estimates due to its unoptimized space usage. This inherent limitation is what ultimately causes the algorithm's failure when dealing with adaptive inputs. A previous study discovered that even a single adaptive input can disrupt the CountSketch algorithm's proper functioning. This study investigates how CountSketch handles adaptive input distributions and determines its robustness in such scenarios. It discovers that the algorithm can successfully handle up to polynomially many adaptive inputs of the same magnitude as random inputs without deteriorating its performance. Ultimately, it proposes a revised version of the CountSketch algorithm resilient to adaptive inputs and presents improved inefficient item identification and duplicate detection algorithms based on this improved CountSketch.

Building on previous research, we expand the conditions from characterizing a metric of non-negative scalar curvature that allows splitting along a non-separating hypersurface. The new conditions are also sufficient to guarantee this property. In comparing them to those for isolated points, we remove the requirement that the dimension should be at least four. Additionally, we prove that isolated points with a non-separating hypersurface closure don't exist when the dimension is two or three. We further observe that in three dimensions, these conditions can be simplified to the non-negative scalar curvature of the hypersurface itself.

A liquid containing superconducting vortices and subject to an magnetic field exhibits a complex behavior that can be modeled as a liquid with entropy-carrying particles. Vortents, the quantum entanglements, play a crucial role in this system. When the vortices cross, they result in the entanglement's annihilation, leading to entropy production. The recombination of a vortex pair, in turn, causes the disappearance of ental and a shift in the local temperature, ultimately giving rise to an entropy flow, all of which are incorporated into the two-fluid hydrodynamic equations for such a system. A hydrodynamic model, accounting for these factors, is then developed, leading to an analysis of the resulting forces in steady-state scenarios. The model's application to the vortex liquid, in turn, enables the prediction of observable phenomena, including the occurrence of a third critical velocity in the Reissner-Nordstr\"om star, as well as the basis for the Nernst effect, seen in rotating superconductors, to be understood.

The control of complex systems with multiple interconnected components poses a significant challenge, particularly when the underlying dynamics are highly nonlinear and subject to external influences. Often, optimal control is contingent upon precise knowledge of system parameters, which are not always obtainable in real-world applications. In this research, a novel approach known as learned flexibility is proposed to address this challenge. By separating optimal control into two distinct aspects, namely optimal real-time control and optimal offline planning, this method identifies a region of feasible solutions that can be efficiently solved using semidefinite programming. A case study on predicting and controlling traffic patterns in a smart city demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach, yielding robust and stable traffic control even in the presence of unpredictable external factors.

The rise of deep learning techniques has enabled the development of sophisticated algorithms that can automate stock trading and optimize portfolio performance.

One prominent approach, known as deep reinforcement learning, has yielded impressive results in forecasting stock prices and making informed investment decisions.

In this project, we explored a hybrid method combining a language model called BERT with a generation-adversarial network to analyze news articles and forecast stock prices, using a dataset from Yahoo Finance comprising IBM stock data from 2007 to 2017.

Our results showed that this hybrid method outperformed a traditional LSTM baseline, achieving higher returns and lower drawdowns in backtests, while also demonstrating robustness in stock selection and the impact of using only positive or negative news on portfolio performance.

This study introduces SCATTER, a cutting-edge universal envelope formalism based on the time correlation of scattering signals to analyze dynamic processes. A key innovation of SCATTER is the calculation of a dimensionless time correlation matrix using a high-speed, low-latency algorithm, available as a standalone application and integrated with major spectroscopy packages on top of GBS. The SCATTER algorithm's efficiency and versatility are demonstrated through the investigation of complex processes such as electron scattering in argon, electron dissociation of acetylene, and ionization of cyclopropane, in various states of ionization.

Research on double Higgs boson production in future TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ colliders using Effective Field Theories can highly enhance our understanding of the Higgs sector. This study investigates the potential of DHH in the Effective Field Theories framework to discern new physics beyond the Standard Model, specifically the nature of Higgs interactions. We analyze the impact of Higgs self-interactions on the shape of the effective potential and Higgs production mechanisms. By researching the potential for Higgs pair production at the International Linear Collider and the European Linear Collider, we find that while certain final states may face detection challenges, others such as $b\bar{b}\tau^+\tau^-$ and $b\bar{b}T_T$ could still offer promising avenues for studying EFT effects.

We successfully identify the correct mathematical framework for constructing non kinetic gravity Lagrangians, utilizing a non-cinetic Stueckelberg-Lagrange formalism. By applying this method, we can develop gravity Lagrangians from arbitrary primary and non-cinetic constraints, without needing to consider the specific structure of those constraints. In the process, a general formula is derived for calculating the Stueckelberg-Lagrange multipliers from the kinetic constraints alone.

A new computational framework has been developed to model localized shocks traveling within a five-dimensional space that mimics the behavior of the AdS metric. This framework uses a series of equations based on spatial variations to describe the behavior of the AdS metric after the intersection of two plane shock waves traveling in perpendicular directions. The method produces highly accurate results, with the residual error falling within the range of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$ when the strength of the shock is small. Notably, the framework reveals that certain initial conditions lead to the formation of singularities, while other conditions result in the propagation of an expanding cocoon-like wavefront. Furthermore, a detailed examination of the framework's behavior near points where localized shocks intersect has provided an in-depth understanding of the phenomenon.

We investigated the drag forces acting on a cylindrical object as it moves through a granular bed, considering its velocity at various angles relative to the object's long axis. Using discrete element method simulations, we analyzed the drag forces based on the Reynolds and Archimedes numbers. Our results showed a anisotropic pattern of drag forces, particularly at low Reynolds numbers, with the cylinder experiencing the highest drag when moving along its long axis and the lowest when moving across its transverse axis. This anisotropy was found to be more pronounced in beds with smaller aspect ratios. Moreover, the drag forces demonstrated hysteresis effects, with the cylinder's orientation significantly impacting the drag forces it endured.

A starbursting disk galaxy named IC 3598A, located 6500 megaparsecs away, is exhibiting signs of a star formation rate of 0.41 solar masses per year, fueled by a collection of supermassive point sources. Recent simulations suggest that intense outflows from these sources may be responsible for regulating the galaxy's star formation rate. To investigate this hypothesis, a team utilized high-resolution data from the ALMA and Chandra to examine the distribution of molecular gas, atomic gas, and X-ray emissions, as well as outflows, within the galaxy. They discovered a negative correlation between molecular gas and X-ray emissions, a negative correlation between atomic gas and outflows, and a positive correlation between molecular gas and large-scale outflows, all of which align with a model where the galaxy's star formation is a result of competition between a top-down process, driven by gas accretion and a local process, driven by gas ejection and waste management in zones of high star formation. Interestingly, the observed outflows are consistent with large-scale phenomena but not with smaller outflows expected from individual point sources. A re-evaluation of the data using a more robust statistical approach suggests the galaxy's visible mass is being balanced by dark matter on both inner and outer scales of rotation.

Organized Bayesian Optimization (Obabo) is a new technique that utilizes log files to apply Bayesian Optimization (BO) to complex systems with numerous parameters. These systems are often too intricate for straightforward optimization methods due to their extensive number of parameters. We now present Organized Bayesian Optimization (Obabo) as a novel approach to facilitate the efficient optimization of such systems. Obabo achieves this by structuring the parameter space into smaller, manageable groups and utilizing Asynchronous Parallel BO (APBO) to optimize each group simultaneously. We developed an early version of Obabo called BoGraph and created it as an extension to the Organized Data Framework. In a practical demonstration, we organized log files from the intricate tuning of a machine learning model's hyperparameters and applied Obabo to efficiently find the optimal hyperparameters.

Our research findings, based on a multiphase transport model calculation, indicate that triangular flow $v_3$ produced in 2013 Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions aligns with turbulent viscosity predictions. However, this is in contrast to laboratory viscosity measurements, which show significant discrepancies. Additionally, contrary to well-established conclusions, this study finds that the initial spatial anisotropy is not a prerequisite for three-fold symmetric flow development.

The quality of web data has consistently deteriorated over time, which has
consequently diminished the effectiveness of the Semantic Web in improving
online discovery and decision-making processes.  Assessing and improving data
quality has become an essential task for both engineers and researchers, yet this
remains a challenging task due to the vast number of rules needed for a
comprehensive evaluation and the difficulty in applying these rules to graph
structures.  We developed QUALIDON, a method for generating high-quality
assessments of large-scale RDF datasets by combining both manual and automated
techniques.  Our approach includes developing customizable quality indicators,
analyzing the data structure to identify applicable verification methods, and
demonstrating the framework's efficacy through the evaluation of nine sizable
RDF datasets representing various domains.

Establishing reliable parameter estimates for stochastic processes under linear and line-shaped observations is crucial in the analysis of dynamic systems. Line-shaped data is frequently encountered in applications such as spectroscopy, but its parameter estimation can be challenging due to the line's orientation and slant. This research introduces modified versions of M- and L-norms specifically tailored to continuous parameter vectors that define a line in two-dimensional space under discrete data observations. These adaptations enable the use of Monte Carlo simulation for initial values, thus avoiding the convergence issues associated with traditional maximum likelihood estimation methods. The efficacy and robustness of the proposed methods are validated through the assessment of bias, mean squared error, and resistance to outlying observations under diverse data observation scenarios. The study's methods are demonstrated through the estimation of the parameters of a bivariate linear regression under discrete observations, but the approach can be applied to any stochastic process under a linear line.

This analysis of six Seyfert galaxies with narrow-line regions showing a pronounced tilt reveals an unexpected feature. In four cases, the narrow-line emission outside the major tilt axis displays characteristics of shock emission, characterized by strong [S II] and weak [N II]. This pattern is indicative of something external influencing the ionized gas, potentially due to interaction with another galaxy or accretion of cool gas. Furthermore, the data shows that narrow-line gas tends to align with large-scale spiral structures in disk galaxies. This alignment may indicate that the ionized gas experiences drag forces and tends to follow the path of maximum density within the galaxy disk. This observed behavior supports previous hypotheses suggesting that the ionized gas in spiral galaxies tends to align with the galaxy disk.

Current evaluation methods for machine learning models on mobile devices and other types of limited resources platforms are not suitable, as they assume idealized conditions that do not reflect real-world scenarios. To accurately assess model performance in these environments, we developed a new evaluation system called EDDIE that utilizes real-world data sources such as conversations, music recordings, and text messages. EDDIE can be easily adapted to any machine learning application by using real data that matches the particular domain being studied. We tested the effectiveness of our system by evaluating three machine learning models on mobile devices and compared the results with laboratory tests and measurements taken in a controlled environment. Our research shows that our approach provides the most accurate representation of a model's actual performance in a resource-constrained environment.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider has achieved significant breakthrough理解 in the realm of beauty meson research, extending beyond the scope of LHC startup studies. Notable discoveries and precise measurements, such as neutrino charge conjugation violation in the beauty meson system, including R/DK and neutral beauty meson mixing parameters, were attained. Furthermore, the experiment has set stringent limits on highly suppressed charm and beauty meson decay modes. These accomplishments are attributable to an expansive data sample, accumulated over multiple runs on the LHC, as well as specialized triggering and reconstruction techniques, customized analysis methods, and the incorporation of theoretical input from beauty factory experiments and global fitting efforts.

The production of realistic traffic scenarios is crucial for training and assessing
traffic supervision models, which are often trained on large quantities of annotated data.
Traditionally, this process involved annotating a significant number of real-world images,
but it became increasingly expensive and time-consuming as the dataset size expanded.
We propose SceneGen, a traffic scene generation framework, designed to rapidly generate
extensive numbers of realistic traffic scenarios, potentially in large datasets. SceneGen
is based on the concept of implicit neural style transfer, but it is specifically
tailored for traffic scenes and executes on a GPU, enabling it to generate multiple
realistic traffic scenarios in quick succession. We evaluate the quality of the generated
scenarios using a combination of metric-based assessment and human testing, and we
demonstrate that SceneGen can be utilized to generate significantly large quantities of
realistic traffic scenarios, and we have employed it to generate over 80,000 scenarios
from just 10,000 base images across three datasets.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic weak Gibbs measures that are related to the long-range interactions. A key property of these measures is that their periodicity depends not on the tree's branching factor, but rather on the oscillation of its edge weights over distance layers. If the weights form a periodic pattern with period $k$, and $d$ (where $d$ is an odd number greater than two) does not divide $k$, then there exists a unique weak Gibbs state with that period $k$. Furthermore, a specific construction of edge weights guarantees the uniqueness of the periodic weak Gibbs measures.

This study investigates using preconditioned Krylov subspace techniques to solve high-dimensional systems created by structure-preserving discretisations, which transform PDEs into equivalent forms. We focus on two commonly employed structure-preserving methods: symplectic multisymplectic schemes for Hamiltonian PDEs, and compactly supported compact absorption (CSAC) multisymplectic schemes for nonlinear dissipation PDEs. The effectiveness of iteratively solving these structures is examined, alongside comparing their performance to an alternative iterative solver. Notable successes with preconditioned multisymplectic methods are demonstrated for various test cases.

Let $T$ be a measure preserving transformation on the area, and let $f$ be a $T$-invariant function with an average value of 1. This paper addresses the question of whether the time average of $f$ at the orbit of an arbitrary point $x$, denoted as $f_n(x) := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f(T^j(x))$, converges to 1 almost everywhere with respect to $\mu$, where $\mu$ is the $T$ invariant measure. This problem was initially explored by F. Schweitzer in 1974, who provided examples illustrating that individual ergodic sequences may not always behave as expected. This article aims to demonstrate that if the sequences generated by $T$ on $f$ are ergodic with a given probability, then the combined sequence is also ergodic with a given probability. As a direct application of this theorem, it is shown that if $T$ is exact and $f$ is mixing with a mean value of 1, or if $T$ is mixing and $f$ is exact, then the system generated by $T$ on $f$ exhibits $\mu$-a.e. exactness.

We investigated the interaction between low-metallicity stellar outflows and molecular cloud environments to better understand how quickly dust forms during early stages of cosmic history. By modeling this process, and referencing specific scenarios like those in the early universe and nearby galaxies, we assessed the formation of dust during low-metallicity supernova events. Our results demonstrate that dust created by supernovae can account for observed abundances if the surrounding environment effectively traps the explosive debris within a short period of time. Furthermore, we found that adding the influence of the host star's radiation to our models allows them to more accurately represent observed data, particularly in cases involving supernovae.

Developing a far-field 3D identification system is an essential step in creating effective remote user authentication applications, yet existing approaches struggle to perform well at considerable distances. We tackled this issue by releasing the Far3Det dataset, a new benchmark for far-field 3D identification in roaming scenarios up to 8 meters. Existing datasets are limited to 2 meters or less, preventing research on the far-field 3D identification problem. We investigated several existing methods for far-field 2D identification and found them inadequate, as they either fail to handle varying lighting conditions, require users to move closer, or perform poorly in 3D scenarios. We explored three existing approaches for 3D identification in the far-field and found them unsuccessful. Consequently, we proposed a novel framework called LightFlow, which achieves state-of-the-art performance at 6 meters in both 2D and 3D scenarios, outperforming other methods by a significant margin in 3D scenarios at 6 meters.

We propose a quantum machine learning approach to ground state approximation in a compound system, building upon a proof of principle that an ansatz for the ground state can be derived from the individual component systems. This new framework leverages a classical machine learning model to predict the parameters of a quantum circuit, significantly reducing the search space and preventing local minima issues. It also allows for the application of advanced classical optimization techniques. Although initially demonstrated with a 1D Heisenberg model, this approach can be adapted to other compound systems, potentially bringing the early stages of quantum machine learning within reach of near-term quantum computers.

Non-rigid registration is an essential process in aligning medical images for analysis and monitoring of patient conditions. This study focuses on developing a non-rigid method to match volume imaging data with surface data. The proposed approach employs a novel framework that utilizes biomechanical modeling to map the relationship between volume and surface images, streamlining the registration process. By utilizing pre-trained models, the method allows for efficient use of various imaging modalities and minimizes the need to solve complex equations. The research presents two strategies for joint matching of images and incorporates an intermodality transformation to accommodate differences in modality. The method was tested on real-world datasets and demonstrated superior results compared to existing techniques.

For a stationary, spherically symmetric space described by a generic metric, our study identifies the conformal Killing vectors associated with its energy-momentum tensor. Moreover, we classify all possible conformal symmetries and the underlying conformal algebra at this level.

This study focuses on developing a self-supervised 3D flow estimation method for autonomous vehicles, utilizing 3D lidar data. We present a novel metric learning approach that enables the extraction of an efficient scene flow model by learning a distance metric in the 3D lidar data space. However, we discovered through experimentation that using 3D lidar data alone results in an approach vulnerable to errors from recognition mistakes and ambient conditions, leading to adversarial effects that compromise the performance of the encoding network and the distance metric learner. Consequently, we discovered that training the recognition and metric learning components jointly with adversarial objectives yields diminishing returns and ultimately produces worse outcomes than treating the problem as a straightforward unsupervised metric learning task.

In recent years, AI networks have achieved remarkable success in a wide range of applications. However, their high computational demands and low energy efficiency pose significant challenges. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive solution by mimicking the natural way neurons process information and signaling, resulting in higher computational efficiency and lower energy consumption. Despite considerable research into SNNs, key challenges persist, encompassing issues with training methods, lack of robust benchmarking procedures, and high classification errors. To address these problems, we introduce the Random Neural Network with Pseudo-time Unfolded Training (RNN-PUT) model, an innovative approach that leverages the strengths of both traditional and spiking models. By integrating the flexibility of conventional random neural networks with the energy efficiency of SNNs, our method drastically reduces errors and lowers energy consumption when compared to existing SNN benchmarks. Notably, our approach achieves a 10x decrease in errors during MNIST classification and a 2.5x reduction in energy consumption when classifying more complex images.

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark stars that have been stabilized by compacting with a strong magnetic field under conditions of finite temperature. By applying the grand canonical ensemble and considering the spin and flavor composition of the quarks, we derived the spin-polarized strange quark star equation of state, taking into account the interactions between the magnetic field and the intrinsic magnetic moments of the quarks. This derived equation of state was then used to investigate the thermal stability and thermal oscillation modes of these quark stars through the analysis of their mass-radius and mass-central density relationships.

A graph that contains a perfect matching aligned with a given Hamiltonian path is known as an ideal matching. This property has been extensively studied since the introduction of Snarks by Tait in 1867 and the introduction of ideal snarks in 2015 led to investigations into graphs that possess ideal Snark colourings. Researchers have since discovered numerous cubic graphs on specific families, such as Heawood graphs, that are both ideal snarks and 4-edge colourable by their entire edge set. This paper presents an algorithm to identify ideal matchings within a particular class of cubic graphs, and as a byproduct, provides improved results regarding the inclusion of certain graphs in ideal matchings and Hamiltonian cycles.

We investigate the connection between arrangements of geometric blocks in the real plane and whether certain quadratic polynomials can take prime values infinitely often. A key result comes from Davenport and Schinzel, showing that if strict triangles exist within an infinite arrangement of real blocks, the quadratic polynomial $n^2 + n + 41$ can take prime values infinitely often. This is extended to include cases where some blocks may be degenerate. A key observation is that the ability of quadratic polynomials to take prime values infinitely often is closely linked to the ability of block arrangements to define points on those blocks for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The research also establishes the d-nosability of certain pentagonal block arrangements and explores the n-representability of various other block arrangements. A key theorem is the introduction of the concept of "shifted blocks" and the subsequent "shift theorem," allowing the infinite no-go region for n-representability to be expanded.

This paper introduces Timeloops, a novel approach to optimizing containerized microservices through intelligent system call scheduling.  It automatically suggests high-performance file system call sequences that are robust and reliable for various applications.  Through a closed-loop performance evaluation process, Timeloops assesses the practical effectiveness of these suggested call sequences, demonstrating superior speed compared to standard scheduling methods across multiple benchmarks.

Investigating extensions of the Standard Model that incorporate a B-L gauge symmetry is an intriguing area of study, prompting numerous proposals to include additional gauge fields beyond the diagonal elements. Within an extension of the Standard Model that includes two such extra gauge fields, we examine a scenario in which one of them is linked to the B-L symmetry. By introducing the corresponding Higgs fields, we are able to break the electroweak and B-L symmetries, thus producing the Higgs boson as a pseudo-Goldstone boson. The two additional gauge fields are successfully confined within the TeV energy range, providing a mechanism for dark matter stability. The collision of the cosmic reheating temperature with the pseudo-CPP scale offers a viable mechanism for dark matter production through scatterings of thermal origin. The proposed model is in line with the observed dark matter density and the B-L breaking scale, while remaining consistent with the measured masses of the W and Z bosons and the pseudo-Goldstone Higgs boson's mass.

This study examines a continuous-discrete version of the PMBM filter that utilizes an origin model, where targets are generated at fixed known positions using a point process derived from an image, and explores using an alternative approach to origin model, Duda's technique.  Using a point process based origin model, a new method for updating the intensity measure after sensor data is presented and a fixed grid-based origin model is analyzed for its mathematical equivalence, implications on the filter parameters, and use cases in sensor management.  These applications are supported by a case study involving space debris monitoring.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model subject to interior decay, described by the equation $u_t - \Delta u = \lambda \Delta_{\mathcal{M}}u(f(u) + h) in\ \Omega\times\Omega_{T}$, with $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega\times\Omega_{T}$ and $h$ supported within a subdomain $\omega$ of $\Omega$. The research establishes that null controllability holds for all non-negative values of $\lambda$, with the key implication being the ability to drive the population $u$ to extinction in a finite time by introducing an external source $h$. The connection to a related control problem, which seeks to maximize the population given an interior source, is also discussed.

In soccer games, teams often struggle to execute coordinated maneuvers during high-stakes situations, hindering their overall performance. This paper presents a method to improve players' actions during such situations by analyzing ball trajectories. A Markov Decision Process model is used to evaluate player actions, and a neural network-based approach is employed to train a policy that can make decisions based on the positions of the ball and teammates, as well as the opposition. To tackle the challenges associated with interpreting continuous data, we introduce two innovations: the use of action embeddings and the application of localized activation functions. These improvements enable the model to learn effective actions, including essential techniques such as passing, shooting, and marking, and facilitates communication among players through a mechanism of action anticipation. Our method is tested on a publicly available soccer dataset, showing significant gains in simulation results.

For high-resolution imaging of large objects that emit known signals, traditional methods often fail due to signal cross-talk. This research proposes an innovative approach utilizing a novel strategy to accurately recover the emitted signals of an extended source in the time-domain. The proposed method involves a two-step process, starting with an initial broad estimation of the source's characteristics, followed by a more precise application of cross-correlation techniques to a smaller, focused area. This approach is demonstrated through both numerical simulations and experimental tests on a large-scale transmission line model.

We demonstrate the creation of optical asymmetry in a mirror-like substance through the process of quantum squeezing. This is achieved via a single-mode system, where a balanced mixture of vortices and anti-vortices results in optical asymmetry. By adjusting the mixture ratio, we can control the extent of optical asymmetry. A key characteristic of our model is its ability to create optical asymmetry in the absence of any external influence or time-reversal disruption. Furthermore, we exhibit a phenomenon of optical directionality switching induced by quantum squeezing, and propose a method for efficient quadratic squeezing in a practical scenario.

We present the first observation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary IGR J19294+1816 in the soft gamma-ray burst state, which is the focus of this study. The data were collected in August 2019, when the source re-emerged after its previous appearances in 2017 and the first half of 2018, all of which were documented in the paper and the associated references. The spectrum of the source is well explained by a two-temperature plasma model during the observation, which is consistent with the findings of the earlier study. The temperature of the base plasma is 2.4 keV. Additionally, the analysis of X-ray light curves and power density spectra revealed the presence of two quasi-periodic oscillations at frequencies of 0.14 Hz and 0.21 Hz. The narrower QPO exhibits an amplitude of 18% and a Gaussian equivalent width of a cyclotron line at an energy of 27.5 keV was detected in the higher energy range of the spectrum. The parameters of this line were estimated to be an equivalent width of 2.4 keV, an intensity of 2.4 x 10-3, and a cyclotron energy of 27.5 keV. The results of this study are discussed in the context of current theoretical models of pulsar spectra.

This study develops a probabilistic model combining noise and diffusion to examine species dynamics in an electoral framework, revealing how species competition and colonization influence the species distribution. By applying a stochastic PDE approach, the model reveals how the species distribution is affected by a key factor - a parameter that determines the balance between mutual species interaction and colonization, and influences the species coexistence or dominant species exclusion.

This article introduces Suryakala-Nusantara, a comprehensive database of 
Indonesian sundials from various historical periods. Sundials are timekeeping 
devices that rely on the movement of the Sun to cast shadows and indicate time. 
Indonesian sundials have unique names, often derived from the names of royal 
families who owned them, and they serve as a significant cultural artifact. 
Despite their historical and scientific value, many sundials have been discarded 
or damaged due to a lack of awareness about their worth. To mitigate this, 
preservation efforts are being promoted through initiatives like creating 
digital replicas of sundials and incorporating them into educational tools for 
Indonesian children. Additionally, a sun path calculator tool has been developed 
to assist users in understanding the movement of the Sun and its relationship 
with sundials, ultimately aiding in the preservation and promotion of this 
timekeeping technology in Indonesia.

This research explores a novel concept of a reflecting surface that adapts to human behavior in an integrated data and energy network with D2D communications. A multi-user system is examined where some surfaces modify their cognitive states to maximize power transfer, while others maintain a balance between power transfer and information delivery by adjusting their reflecting patterns. Optimization techniques are implemented to achieve a stable state of equilibrium, and the resulting energy and information rates are calculated for both types of users. Furthermore, the cognitive nature of the reflecting surfaces influences the achievement of an optimal solution that maximizes information data rates and power transfer efficiency.

This paper presents an innovative approach to obtaining two-dimensional coordinate data of distant objects using a 2D LDV system. The proposed system overcomes the limitations of conventional LDV technology, which can only obtain depth information. By integrating an LDV with photogrammetry, our solution successfully bridges the photogrammetry calibration process, allowing for photogrammetry to function without prior calibration. Furthermore, the system is capable of 2D coordinate data acquisition from distant points, even when observers and photogrammetrists are not visible in the scene. As an example, the proposed system was utilized to measure the two-dimensional coordinates of a bridge located 60 meters away.

The limited coherence of modern transmission electron microscopes (TEMs) significantly hampers their spatial resolution potential. Researchers are increasingly utilizing programmable phase plates (PPPs) to broaden the illumination cone in TEMs, yet this approach may also induce scattering that distorts the phase of electrons. To investigate the extent to which a programmable phase plate can compensate for the incoherence-induced limitations, a model is presented that accounts for the combined effects of multislit illumination and a PPP on the spatial resolution of a two-lens TEM. Analytical and numerical results indicate that while a programmable phase plate can enhance the spatial resolution over a certain energy range, its benefits are negated when the plate induces scattering that corresponds to the resolution of the microscope's objective lens. The model is further applied to a specific case study, utilizing a multi-slits PPP developed by the author's group, which illuminates a two-dimensional superposition of hexagonal and square gratings and contains up to the 11th order Bragg peaks. Notably, although the programmable phase plate can induce a more pronounced diffraction pattern and a more detailed difference image, it fails to restore the original square shape of one of the gratings due to its lower order Bragg peaks.

In contrast, our work examines the encoder representations of a generative dialogue model that generates entire dialogue sequences in isolation. We propose an exploratory study to analyze what encoder representations capture in isolation versus in the context of a multi-turn dialogue. We investigate whether the encoding of a single utterance conveys enough background context to predict the next response. We explore the relationship between encoding quality and model performance.
