This paper presents a novel approach to enhance musical instrument recognition by utilizing a hierarchical classification system and adapting Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to accommodate a limited number of sample categories. A pre-trained, multi-class CNN model is adapted to a few-shot classifier by removing irrelevant layers and appending new layers for specific target classes. A hand-crafted hierarchical tree is created to organize the relationships between different instruments, and the multi-class classifier is employed to classify branches of the tree that contain a few-shot target classes. A thorough evaluation using the MAIDS dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach, resulting in a significant improvement in accuracy compared to standard one-shot classification methods.

Acquiring targeted information from a given source of knowledge is a primary way to access that knowledge.
Answering questions that pertain to a specific domain's cutting-edge developments demands up-to-date knowledge and an understanding of complex subjects.
Currently, most knowledge-seeking question-answering systems depend on initial information in the form of online tutorials, news articles, or lecture content.
In contrast, asking questions about research papers is an essential step in comprehending them.
We examine why creating a specialized question-answering dataset from research papers is a challenging task.
We identify three significant obstacles in this process: the limited expressiveness of paper text, the inconsistency in question-answering styles, and the inconsistency in information quality.
To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage framework to extract high-quality knowledge from research papers.
This framework is designed to capture the nuanced, implicit knowledge contained in paper text.
As part of this development process, we introduce QwP-Anto, a comprehensive dataset of over 11,000 specialized questions and answers based on more than 7,000 computer science research papers from top venues.
QwP-Anto can be used to test current question-answering models and provide a foundation for future work in paper-comprehension and the creation of similar datasets.

We estimate the accuracy of calculating the strain power spectral density for a pulsar timing array, inspired by merging eccentric binary systems, using a first-order post-Newtonian expansion of the waveform. Our study compares this method to an exact calculation for binary systems up to four components and semi-analytic approximations for waveform amplitude and orbital period for eccentric binaries. For moderate eccentricities ($e \le 0.6$), the first-order post-Newtonian approximation is within $10\%$ of the exact calculation. For higher eccentricities, the discrepancy increases to around $30\%$. A similar level of accuracy (within $10\%$) is achieved with semi-analytic formulas. These results are applicable to $10^{-10}$-second scale pulsar timing array data and can be extended to shorter scales for future $10^{-11}$-second scale timing arrays.

We analyze the ASEP model on a complete graph to understand particle velocities in relation to initial conditions. This study builds upon earlier research by Balazs and Janowski as well as Seidel, providing a more comprehensive proof using alternative methods. Our approach includes the ability to handle particle configurations on higher-dimensional complete graphs.

This study offers an overview of mathematical methods used to model the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and examines key research areas in this field. Various transmission models are categorized based on underlying assumptions, with a focus on infection dynamics, mobility patterns, and underlying host network structures. We discuss the advantages and constraints of each approach and explore potential pathways for future mathematical modeling of epidemics.

The unique property of a Majorana fermion lies in the fact that it is 
its own antiparticle, which makes it an ideal type of particle for 
fundamental research.  This makes the neutrino, which is a Majorana fermion, 
particularly suitable for study.  However, the fact that neutrinos have 
extremely low mass poses a significant challenge.  To address this, researchers 
often use hypothetical systems of Majorana fermions that are not neutrinos to 
study their characteristics.  To this end, a comprehensive examination of the 
ensemble of non-interacting Majorana fermions was performed, encompassing 
various traits of the system, which can be directly applied to fermionic 
systems of different types.  A key finding of the study was a clear 
relationship between the density of the system and its size, which in turn 
reveals the underlying characteristics of the system and its components.

Acronyms serve as a widely used abbreviation technique in technical and scientific domains, yet they pose significant challenges in text mining tasks due to their prevalence and occasional confusion, especially when different acronyms share the same form and their meanings are not readily apparent from surrounding context. To address this issue, a novel approach called the Disambiguation of Acronym Denotations with Deep contextual Language models framework has gained popularity, involving the training of deep contextual language models on corpus-level data and formant separation based on contextual signals. Formantly, a newly developed open-source platform called MadDog has been created to facilitate the study of acronyms by automatically extracting their instances, potential denotations, and related information from textual sources, as well as conducting disambiguation experiments, drawing on a comprehensive web-based service built on the AWS cloud, which provides ready-to-use sub-analyzes for specific entities and is made available to the research community through its open-source code and flexible, customizable nature.

Converting two spinless atoms into a molecule with an odd number of electrons is
achieved with a direct, three-body process that conserves total electron angular
momentum.  A similar scheme is proposed for converting spinful fermions into an
even-electron molecule by applying a counter-intuitive method: two loosely
bound atoms are first made to strongly interact, and then an external field is
gradually removed to increase the equivalent quantum flux through a virtual
electron orbit.  This process is demonstrated feasible in a triple alkali system,
specifically using lithium-sodium-rubidium mixtures, and might be achievable in
the future with experiments involving cesium.  The proposed method has the
advantage of direct access to the deep, non-adiabatic regions of the atomic
interaction potential, and can be used to create molecules in exotic electronic
states, thus providing a useful alternative to other methods like Feshbach
resonances, photodissociation, and radiative association.

Current storage systems are organized hierarchically to facilitate easy navigation and management. Researchers have recently explored using DNA as a storage medium, recognizing its immense data capacity, though they have yet to leverage its strengths for hierarchical storage frameworks. We introduce HiDnaStor, a novel storage system that effectively combines DNA storage with a hierarchical structure. HiDnaStor achieves this by categorizing data into functional groups, creating a sophisticated yet efficient framework that simplifies data management and updates within a hierarchical structure.

The topological properties of wave systems can be categorized into two types: those arising from isolated singular points or surfaces, and those arising from nodal lines within momentum space. Nodal lines, also called "wireman phases," represent a distinct class of topological phenomena. This review examines recent theoretical and experimental investigations into wireman phases, including their relationship to photonic systems. We discuss topological invariants associated with nodal lines, as well as examples of systems exhibiting this phenomenon, including materials and artificial systems. The review discusses the characteristics of nodal lines, as well as their stability and realization in various systems. Notably, we discuss the Clifton-Perry-Joannopoulos nodal line in momentum space, as well as its relationship to large-scale degeneracies and anomalous Hall effects.

This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture called Multi-task Attention directed Network (MAG-Net) for brain tumor identification, utilizing coregistered MRI images from three imaging modalities, including T1-weighted, T1 contrast-enhanced, and T2-weighted images. MAG-Net is designed to handle both tumor segmentation and image classification simultaneously. The model incorporates a multi-task learning approach and a directed attention mechanism to prioritize relevant features for a specific output. Trained on the Benihanna dataset, MAG-Net demonstrated enhanced accuracy in identifying tumors compared to existing methods, achieving an overall Dice similarity coefficient of 0.855, a sensitivity of 0.855, a precision of 0.855, and a recall of 0.855, while also correctly classifying 0.9858 cases out of test images.

Differentiable programming frameworks have gained popularity in solving inverse problems due to their ability to seamlessly integrate prior knowledge about the problem and the involved operators. However, the computation of the 'shadow' term in the backward pass of certain popular models remains a bottleneck, as it typically involves inverting large matrices. We propose an alternative approach that bypasses this shadow computation altogether. By reformulating the model within the same framework and leveraging the common structure of the model's linear operator, our new approach results in a straightforward reparametrization. This change maintains the same optimization properties and theoretical guarantees while being 10 to 100 times faster in execution. Our proposed solution can be directly implemented in popular differentiable programming models and demonstrates significant performance improvements in various applications, such as image deblurring and magnetic resonance imaging. In fact, in the latter application, our approach outperforms the original model by achieving a 20 dB gain in performance.

A deep deinterlacing method has been developed that effectively removes deinterlacing artifacts in real-time. Utilizing 2x interlaced frames as input, this network learns an intricate mapping between pairs of frames and output pixels at sub-pixel precision. By integrating optical flow with a fully connected layer, it achieves sub-pixel precision. Evaluation on the 1080p30 TV10 segment of the TV-Deinterlacing Track of HMDE 2019 confirms its accuracy. By training on public data, the proposed architecture surpasses existing real-time algorithms and performs comparably to top-performing non-real-time methods. An open-source implementation is available on GitHub.

Our research determined the average square radius of the neutron distribution for 165 radioactive nuclei and 6 stable nuclei with neutron diffusion across their surfaces. By directly comparing experimental data with the results obtained from charge radii calculations using both Skyrme forces and relativistic mean field theory, we found that the average square radius of the neutron distribution can be accurately predicted through the sum of the average square radius of the proton distribution and the difference between the neutron and proton mean field energies, validating the fulfillment of the non-relativistic and relativistic sum rules in our study.

This paper introduces an innovative application of deep learning to rapidly solve the
complex and turbulent shallow water equations, which are used to model the movement of
large bodies of water. By combining a simple scheme with careful analysis, our method
achieves stable and accurate results in solving these equations. The deep learning model
learned to replicate the outcomes of this scheme for both smooth and turbulent river
flows, as well as for the drainage of a flat area. The results show that our model can
accurately predict river flow rates and water depths, as well as the drainage process, in
line with high-fidelity laboratory measurements. The research demonstrates the
potential for using deep learning to solve complex fluid dynamics problems, and paves
the way for further exploration of this approach in hydrodynamics.

High dynamic range photography accommodates a wide spectrum of brightness levels in a scene, accommodating elements both intensely bright and deeply dim. Traditional photography techniques employ multiple exposures of a scene at varying intensity levels, captured either simultaneously or sequentially. Nonetheless, these approaches demand either precise exposure categorization in pre-configured scenarios or the capability to process images one by one. In this research, a novel framework is introduced that automatically determines the optimal approach for high dynamic range photography in urban settings, utilizing a camera found in a standard smartphone. The proposed framework's framework was evaluated using a dataset containing 150 distinct settings, and its capability to produce clear high dynamic range images was assessed.

Artificial Neural Networks are driving significant advancements across various fields, yet they consume substantial amounts of energy, generating nearly 1% of global $CO_2$ emissions in a short span. To mitigate this environmental impact, researchers are exploring methods to deeply train models using fewer resources, specifically causal learning. Causal learning allows for accurate model training on limited data by incorporating external knowledge about data interrelationships. We investigate the use of Causal Profound Learning (CPL) to train complex models like Transformers and Dense Estimators for classification and regression on small datasets. Our findings reveal that CPL enables highly competitive model performance, surpassing single-task learning, while being energy-efficient by reducing training time and environmental impact. We demonstrate that simple causal interventions can lead to robust model performance, making causal learning a promising approach for developing sustainable artificial intelligence systems.

Understanding how temperature behaves in catalytic reactions is crucial for the design of efficient systems, yet existing methods for measuring temperature have significant limitations in providing real-time, three-dimensional data. In this study, we present an innovative approach for obtaining temperature maps in fixed beds using rapid magnetic resonance imaging. By integrating this technique with the placement of non-pyrogenic coils, we can collect high-resolution temperature images in three dimensions, revealing a layered temperature distribution in the flow direction. These findings align well with thermodynamic principles and have implications for the design of efficient reactors for processes requiring precise temperature control.

In the context of high-genus Riemann surfaces, the $b$-principle yields intriguing findings.  However, for curves of genus 3 or higher, a single exception occurs when considering rational coefficients.  This exception is due to the existence of a single, highly intricate torsion element within the cohomology of the modular curve $\mathcal{M}_g$, whose complexity grows exponentially with genus $g$.  This element, denoted as $T_g$, has a known form for genus $g=2$, consisting of two components of orders 2 and 3, respectively.  It appears that $T_2$ has multiple occurrences within families of modular curves of genus 2, but further instances vanish as the genus increases beyond 2.  Therefore, the behavior of the $b$-principle on Riemann surfaces is better described as fragile.  This paper seeks to provide a foundation for addressing fundamental questions regarding the torsion structure of the modular curve $\mathcal{M}_g$.  It introduces the notion of stable torsion, formulates the conjecture that stable orders are finite, and reviews the progress made toward determining the torsion structure of the modular curve $\mathcal{M}_g$.

This research involves a detailed comparison of the computational efficiency of various multilevel multigrid methods for cardiac mechanics, specifically focusing on B-level MMG and traditional T-level TMG. By examining B-L2, modified Corfield-Le Trelles, and Simo-Tarrazon formulations, the authors aim to evaluate how each approach affects computation time and accuracy. Although evaluating multilevel formulations can be more accurate than traditional T-formulations, it often results in increased computation times. Conversely, certain modified traditional solvers have been shown to maintain a balance between accuracy and computation efficiency.

The asymptotic behavior of large $N$ random matrix ensembles is extensively studied, often summarized by their moment sequences. Researchers typically construct specific random matrix models to analyze these behaviors. In this study, we develop a novel class of independent random matrix models applicable to both Hermitian and non-Hermitian scenarios. These models utilize arbitrary distributions for their entries and are suitable for the analysis of their eigenvalues and entry values through non-crossing and generalized partitions, as demonstrated with $2\times 2$ block matrices. A key application involves even deeper trees of correlations in the real symmetric and complex Hermitian ensembles, which may have implications for understanding the landscape of quantum gravity and string theory.

The rise of video content has made it essential for new companies to stay competitive, 
yet the high costs of professional video production can be a significant barrier. 
In response, user-friendly video creation tools based on artificial intelligence have emerged, 
offering a cost-effective alternative. These systems leverage various AI technologies to 
streamline the video creation process, from automatic transcription and summarization 
to emotional analysis and adaptive coding. A comprehensive survey of the latest research 
in AI-driven video production is presented, focusing on the key AI methodologies used 
to enhance video content and improve user engagement. The survey also highlights the 
potential applications of these technologies in advertising and educational settings, 
as well as the challenges and potential directions for future development in this field.

Adversarial defenses are commonly evaluated by measuring the percentage of protected images that are successfully deceived, but this metric is limited as it only considers binary outcomes and fails to account for the subtlety of a protected image's false feeling of security. This research introduces a new assessment metric called the False Feeling of Security (FFS), which is grounded in the concept of security distance in manifold learning. FFS leverages both geodesic and Euclidean distances to quantify a protected image's false feeling of security in the feature space. A case study was conducted on adversarially protected MNIST images to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Furthermore, introducing the concept of step security distance, the research demonstrates that FFS possesses excellent interpretability and controllability. A more in-depth analysis of the feature space reveals that adversarially protected images often lack a clear semantic meaning. To enhance the controllability of the defense method, a novel metric called directional security distance is also defined. Overall, the proposed evaluation method provides a comprehensive assessment framework for adversarially protected images, going beyond traditional binary evaluation methods.

To investigate novel acoustic phenomena in the micrometric range high-frequency ultrasound, the acoustic metamaterial requires a precisely engineered microstructure smaller than the wavelength of sound. Due to limitations imposed by manufacturing techniques on polymers and metals, this study presents two methods to create complex microstructures in the hundred-of-microns range using two-photon polymerization. By fabricating a "microacoustic metagrating" via two-photon litography and comparing it to a 3D-printed counterpart, the authors demonstrate a functional acoustic metagrating capable of efficiently directing high-frequency ultrasound at 2.1 MHz. This capability paves the way for pioneering applications in imaging and the exploration of new acoustic phenomena in the micrometric range high-frequency ultrasound metamaterials.

We investigate how diffusion spreads in ways that deviate from normal, symmetric patterns due to randomly changing diffusion rates, which can occur in various materials and environments.

By combining the fractional heat equation with a randomly varying diffusion rate, we create a new type of equation that describes this kind of deviant diffusion. It is shown that this equation can be solved using an existing solution from Scher and Montroll's work on continuously changing rates of diffusion.

Furthermore, our derivation connects this deviant diffusion to a specific form of process-tracking graph known as a directed scale-free line graph. Using this connection, we can derive a mathematical formula for the typical spread pattern that reflects the existing experimental data and observations of deviant diffusion.

A fundamental understanding of electro and magnetooptical resonator and waveguide systems is essential for a wide range of applications, including the precise measurement of parameters and the creation of light-matter interactions. A general framework has been developed to calculate key parameters of these systems, specifically those involving the modification of material properties via the Kerr effect. The theory is fully quantum mechanical and includes an assessment of the feasibility of mediating interaction between photons based on resonator or waveguide coupling strength and the magnitude of the Kerr effect. Furthermore, the framework encompasses both normal and anomalous self-interaction of light, allowing for the determination of the effective group index and the self-phase modulation coefficient. It has been demonstrated that the feasibility of achieving a strong interaction between photons is influenced by the type of material used and whether the system is a resonator or waveguide. Additionally, the impact of mode geometry and scale on interaction strength has been analyzed in detail.

This paper builds upon prior research to establish a link between global stability and the existence of specific, unbounded control functions that adhere to a refinement of Hurwitz's lemma, applicable to linear systems of the form $\dot{x}=Ax+Bu$, where the control function $u$ can be unbounded. Additionally, we demonstrate the analogous connection between asymptotic stability and a specific, bounded control function for systems including time-varying matrices $A(t)$ and $B(t)$.

This research utilizes the generative adversarial network method to develop a high-resolution reconstruction model for turbulent flows in a backward-facing step, achieving a detailed reconstruction of Reynolds numbers ranging from 40 to 160. A high-precision CFD model was employed to validate the accuracy of our approach, revealing a successful match in mean flow patterns and flow structure at intermediate Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, a high-precision CFD analysis was conducted to investigate flow dynamics at lower and higher Reynolds numbers, with the former demonstrating the amplification of fluctuations in the mixed layer from its baseline form, and the latter showing the activation of bar-Kolmogorov cascades in the mixing layer.

The success of the Feynman path integral in applying quantum field theory to complex systems has notable limitations due to its reliance on nonanalytic functions, which hinderes inclusion of certain terms, such as the $\theta$-term in the action. This note circumvents this issue by suggesting the adoption of the Feynman wave formula as an equally valid starting point for quantum field theory. Illustrating the equivalence of the two approaches in specific scenarios will aim to prove the wave formula's feasibility.

In current open-world recognition systems, the lack of explicit world boundaries results in impaired confidence calculation and compromised decision-making capabilities. Existing approaches, which rely on geometric or heuristic methods, are limited by their inability to capture complex uncertainty patterns and fail to provide clear, adaptable world boundaries. This study introduces an entirely new, unique framework for characterizing open-world uncertainty and proposes a cutting-edge framework called EDUCE, which utilizes energy functions to model the uncertainty of an open-world scenario. By integrating temperature scaling and Platt's method into the energy function framework, we evaluate EDUCE's performance against temperature-based and margin-based approaches on multiple open-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority in accuracy, open-world sensitivity, and calibration. Furthermore, we extend EDUCE by incorporating pairwise ranking and multi-class margin methods to explore diverse uncertainty representations.

To train reinforcement learning agents on high-frequency sensor data for
long periods, we need to create virtual testing scenarios that closely mimic
real-world conditions. Our new platform, L2Explorer, is an advanced evaluation
system for reinforcement learning based on a fully digital testing scenario.
Built using the Simala simulation framework, it offers a high-quality virtual
environment where the learning algorithm can be continuously refined and
applied to new, unseen testing scenarios. As a result, we provide the best possible
conditions for developing reinforcement learning agents using continuous
frequency sensor data.

Our proposed monitoring and exploration framework for declarative processes, known as DATAS, is centered on process streams. This list of matching rules and input data is dynamically updated in real-time, allowing for adaptive process analysis and monitoring. As a result, key performance indicators and other relevant data can be computed in real-time from the process streams, and these computations are facilitated by a stream processing engine. The DATAS solution incorporates an innovative approach based on this, and a case study on invoice processing demonstrates its effectiveness.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light propagation characteristics change dramatically at certain points, indicating a transition from quasi-bound to broken modes. This phenomenon occurs because the quasiperiodic structure causes a reclassification of modes from localized to extended. Our research indicates that adding transverse heterogeneity to this structure can cause photonic modes to transition from quasi-bound to quasi-bound again, effectively increasing their space. This is achieved by creating an overlap between previously disjoint modes, which can be utilized to manipulate and control photonic quasi-bound states for practical applications in photonic quasicrystals.

Liger, a high-performance video spectrograph, is set to revolutionize the capabilities of the W. M. Keck Observatory in the near future. It is designed to overcome the limitations of previous systems by offering broader wavelength coverage, enhanced data rates, improved signal-to-noise ratios, and the ability to simultaneously observe multiple targets. To fully utilize its potential, Liger will be equipped with advanced video detectors in the near-infrared spectrum and will be optimized for high data rates, enabling it to perform a variety of astronomical experiments. Given the enormous amount of data that Liger is expected to produce, a robust system for processing and managing its output must be developed. This system, known as the Science Data Processing System, will be responsible for handling the flow of data from acquisition to storage, as well as controlling the operation of the spectrograph and processing its output in real-time. A key feature of SDPS is its modular design, which allows for easy adaptation to the evolving needs of the project. Furthermore, the development of the necessary software to support its functions is being carried out by a collaborative team of scientists and engineers from several institutions, working in close coordination with astronomical users and the observatory staff.

Our research showcases the potential of using entangled photon pairs in a new type of spatial mode demultiplexing technique, allowing for precise measurement of small shifts in a diffraction grating beyond its usual limit. By analyzing the two photons' interference patterns, we achieve an remarkable improvement, sensing minute displacements equivalent to just a few nanometers.

This paper offers a statistical examination of ecosystem dynamics using data from over three decades, focusing on two species of birds in an island forest. A distinct two-tiered pattern has emerged in the population dynamics of one species of bird following the sudden appearance of a highly invasive plant. To detect subtle, early warning indicators of such dramatic population shifts, we employed two statistical measures specifically designed for time series data: changes in the ratio of persistent to anti-persistent fluctuations and persistent homology. Both methods successfully identified a significant increase in noise within the leucistic bird's habitat, as well as the precocious appearance of the invasive plant, preceding the epiphyte's population collapse. Our study demonstrates the utility of these statistical approaches in identifying latent, long-lasting transients in ecosystem settings.

Determining whether stellar feedback from a galaxy's core influences the maintenance of a galaxy's bulge mass and star formation rate beyond a certain point is a critical area of study in astronomy. A crucial source of such feedback could be nuclear activity within a galaxy's core, especially since a significant proportion of a galaxy's feedback seems to originate from the nucleus. A vital aspect of investigating the role of nuclei involves analyzing star formation rates and stellar masses specifically within a galaxy's nucleus rather than the whole galaxy. Utilizing a vast dataset encompassing nearly 2000 galaxies in the local universe, spanning a wide star formation rate spectrum, this study explores nuclear star formation patterns in relation to global properties, distinct structural components, and active nuclei. It reveals that the efficiency of star formation within a galaxy's nucleus tends to decline as the stellar mass of the galaxy increases, primarily because a galaxy's halo seems to suppress nuclear star formation rather than the activity within the galaxy's core. Furthermore, active galactic nuclei activity seems to have no significant impact on the formation of stars within a galaxy's core. Consequently, stellar feedback from a galaxy's core alone, without considering the surrounding environment, might not be sufficient to explain the observed pattern of star formation efficiency in a galaxy's bulge.

This paper explores the application of multi-task learning to enhance
performance in sentiment analysis across languages, utilizing available data
from multiple languages during the training process. We specifically examine
the challenges of low-resource languages and the potential benefits of
transfer learning, with the primary objective of accurately predicting
sentiments in a low-resource language such as Catalan. By leveraging abundant
English data for sentiment classification, we aim to improve the classification
of sentiments in Catalan. The results of the experiments demonstrate the
effectiveness of the approach, resulting in notable improvements in
accuracy for Catalan data and negligible differences for English data, when
comparing the outcomes of single-task and multi-task learning. The source code
for the models used in the experiments is made available on GitHub.

The well-known fence downgrading problem arises from a unique scenario in which multiple processes, operating on a shared variable initially set to 1, are tasked with independently deciding whether to lower the fence to 0. This task is complicated by the fact that processes are not guaranteed progress due to the absence of a total ordering mechanism on the fence. Notably, this situation resembles the classic impossibility problem in which at least one process is guaranteed to lower the fence. A novel approach proposed for resolving this issue involves providing a mechanism to invalidate the fence from any state. This enables a downgrading protocol where the fence can be lowered to 0 or 1, depending on the invalidation. We present an innovative design that allows at least one process to successfully lower the fence to 0 or 1 using only O(1) memory. This design can be enhanced to ensure that all processes succeed with the same level of memory efficiency.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem asserts that if integers 'a' and 'b' within the same equivalence class modulo some integer have the same sum, then the number of distinct sums formed by combining two different elements from set A is at least 2|A|-log_2(|A|/k).

This paper examines the measure and topological properties of shifted fractional Brownian motion paths, denoted as $B^H(t)+b$, where $B^H$ follows fractional Brownian motion with a factor $H$ and a fixed positive constant $b$. A key objective is to investigate the nature of the image sets for these paths over the interval $[0,1]$. Our findings aim to address an open question posed by Hawkes regarding the nature of $Im(B^H(t)+b)$ and reveal that when the factor $H$ exceeds 0.5, the image sets possess a positive Lebesgue measure and an interior that is non-empty with probability one.

To apply Dirac's successful time-independent variational principle to various quantum systems, a general form of the Hamiltonian was created. Specifically, the Hamiltonian's structure is defined by the density, kinetic energy, and potential energy components. Using this approach, the effectiveness of a modified, parametric Henon-Heiles model with quantum disorder was examined. H-eigenfunction theory was applied to analyze this modified system, and its results were compared to standard H\'enon-Heiles model functions developed by researchers.

X-ray images can reveal a variety of potential indicators that suggest a patient's likelihood of requiring intensive care, a task that has been an intriguing research topic. This task has been under study in recent years, yet existing datasets used are not representative of real-world scenarios, which result in models that do not perform optimally when applied to real patients. A new comprehensive COVID-19 dataset has been created, consisting of 1549 chest X-rays annotated to reflect actual patient clinical outcomes, which will enable a more accurate evaluation of future models. This dataset is being made publicly available to encourage the development of improved imaging analysis techniques.
We prove that the simplicial collection of group objects within a category already forms a simplicial group within that same category.

Our analysis reveals the VRD task is hindered by a significant problem: many model predictions are incorrect positives. Due to the vast number of possible unconnected object pairs, models frequently identify additional objects in the scene that were not part of the annotated target. This issue is especially pronounced in datasets constructed via simple box crossing, as they generate numerous artificial potential relationships. Even when employing a filtering strategy to remove instances of objects that were not detected, our findings show this is insufficient in effectively eliminating erroneous positives. In order to address this problem, we suggest a new metric called Precise VRD (pVRD) and a corresponding training objective called VRD with Negative Sampling (VRDNS). By including erroneous object pairs as negative samples, pVRD focuses on maximizing the model's probability of correct object pairs and minimizing the probability of incorrect ones. For testing purposes, we utilize all annotated object pairs and detected combinations of objects. To further enhance the data, we introduce Relationship Clean VRD (rcVRD) samples, in which only the objects that were actually detected and had a valid relationship are kept, discarding the rest of the potential object pairs. When we applied VRDNS to the original dataset and the rcVRD samples, the evaluation metrics improved significantly in terms of VRD mean average precision and pVRD mean average precision.

This study introduces an innovative approach to creating robust action recognition models that excel in low-light conditions with limited data. Our proposed method, Delta Sampling R-BERT (DSRB), is based on pre-trained models and incorporates a novel component called the BERT embedding reconstruction module (BERT-BRM). DSRB's BERT-BRM method effectively counteracts the impact of data scarcity and poor lighting on the action recognition model by learning to preserve the distribution of action data under these challenging conditions. Furthermore, we utilize the powerful feature extraction capabilities of the pre-trained model and add a lightweight classification module to create an efficient and accurate action recognition system. Experimental results show that DSRB outperforms existing methods that adapt state-of-the-art models to low-light and data-starved scenarios, especially when only a limited number of actions are tested under these conditions.

This report outlines an experimental Content-Aware Parallel Processing System built on a Field Programmable Gate Array. Traditional content-addressable arrays were surpassed by our innovative design which incorporates parallel processing capabilities. We developed a custom parallel operating system and created a framework for simultaneous, parallel processes to create and access data within the arrays. Furthermore, we successfully implemented several parallel operating system functions including data access, process scheduling, and inter-process communication.

We've analyzed a galaxy at redshift 3.08 that is actively accreting and is part of a low-mass group, appearing to be on the outer edges. It is compact, with an effective radius of 0.6 kiloparsecs, and exhibits asymmetry, with one side showing more light. It has a large effective surface brightness gradient, with one side showing more light. It has a quiescent, lopsided disk, formed from a disk-like component in the inner regions and a substructure trailing behind, likely caused by a tidal interaction. It is associated with gas that is accreting from above, which is also seen in a group. It has a gas-to-stellar mass ratio of more than one, indicating it has more than enough gas to form a gas-dominated galaxy. It has a gas disk that is tilted at an angle of more than 90 degrees compared to the stellar disk, which is also observed in a low-mass disk galaxy at lower redshifts. It has a compact, two-component gas disk, which is distinct from a single-ring structure, likely caused by a tidal interaction. It has a bulge-to-effective radius ratio of more than one, which is more compact than the stellar disk, which is observed in a low-mass galaxy at lower redshifts. This paper aims to analyze the periodic solutions of a specific type of elliptic equation that models scenarios involving heat conduction. For a given domain in high-dimensional space, we investigate whether there are non-trivial solutions to this equation, particularly in light of its connection to a long-standing problem in mathematical analysis known as the Steklov eigenfunction problem. A key finding in our research is that, under certain conditions, the conduction equation has solutions that are multiples of a given function, mirroring a result from a related study. Moreover, our results allow us to partially address a dimensionality-related aspect of the Steklov problem by establishing a connection between eigenvalues and dimensionality. Additionally, we establish a relationship between Steklov coefficients and a specific parameter, offering a bridge between these two areas of mathematical study.

Recent advances in creating programs using machine learning have been most effective when combined with supervision from static analysis techniques, such as verifying correctness and functionality using neural networks and generative techniques. However, there has been limited exploration in integrating the two for both purposes. This study proposes a novel approach of using existing static analysis tools to guide neural networks in generating programs, an idea referred to as meta-guidance. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through enhanced program creation with the help of program analysis techniques, specifically with DOLAB, a neural network-based code generator.

A rare solar event called Neutron Decay Flare (NDF) occurred on November 7, 2004.
This event took place near the limb of the sun and was observed from multiple solar monitoring stations, including SOHO, SDO, and multiple ground-based neutron monitors.
Analysis of this event revealed an X2.0 class flare in the visible spectrum, accompanied by a hard short-duration burst of energy in the direction of high energy photons.
Neutrons are believed to be present at the site of the above mentioned high energy burst, although they cannot be directly detected from Earth.
Our analysis of ground-based data suggests a significant increase in neutron flux at the Earth's surface around the time of the high energy burst, which is consistent with modeling of the propagation of neutrons and their decay products, taking into account Earth's magnetic field and atmospheric effects.
The data also indicates the presence of an Enhanced Air Showers (EAS) flux that could be attributed to the arrival of neutrons, as well as an increased flux of charged particles called protons, which arrived a few minutes later.
However, analysis of data from multiple neutron monitoring stations in the direction of high energy photons suggests a much lower estimate for the initial neutron flux around 60 cm^-2 s^-1, although this estimate does not fully match the observed increase in air showers a few minutes later.

We have computed the dispersion relations for relativistic hydrodynamics, taking into account three types of dissipation: shear, shear-viscous heat flux, and bulk viscous pressure. Notably, the impact of the latter on both ordinary and tachyonic waves is explored. By comparing our computed relations to the linearized dynamics of a scalar field with non-gauge covariant flux term and bulk viscosity, we establish a useful analogy. This analogy also allows us to draw conclusions about the stability conditions of tachyonic systems based on those of the tachyonic scalar field.

Our new anomaly detection method, InQMAD, is designed for use in quantum observations and can also be applied to secure authentication systems based on quantum mechanics. This method is capable of identifying changes in an observation scenario and does so using a learning algorithm that operates with very little data and uses only a single type of measurement across the entire process. In tests using an optical setup, the algorithm's performance was found to match that of more complex approaches, but with the advantage of learning incrementally and with less data.

The question of whether the government can compel the creation of decryption keys is unanswerable without first defining what constitutes a strong encryption system.  To address this ambiguity, we propose a framework that evaluates the strength of an encryption system by comparing it to a system of compromised security measures, or "trustors."  Within this framework, we introduce three models: a system where the government can force a verification of correctness, one where forced decryption occurs, and finally, we explore how these systems relate to each other.  As a source of insight, we use topological concepts to characterize these systems and their connections.  Ultimately, our approach provides a way to define strong encryption systems based on the security of their equivalent system of trustors, or vice versa.  This, in turn, leads to interesting conclusions, such as how the nature of the system of trustors impacts the strength of the encryption system, or how certain topological features of the system affect its security.

We have created a comprehensive simulation tool for the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. This program is versatile and can be utilized to simulate various real-world scenarios, such as asymmetric sources, time-bin single-photon states, and the impact of source and channel imperfections on the source fidelity and quantum bit error rate (QBER). User-defined source states and channelsharings can be input directly into the code, which in turn calculates source fidelity, source anti-correlation, and QBER for both basis settings. By utilizing these parameters, the code can also estimate the final key rate and secure key length as functions of source and channel loss, utilizing pre-amplifiers, and accounting for dark count rates and efficiency mismatch.

Valued decision problems involve calculating a function based on an input that is derived from a function as well. Recent studies on valued decision problems have primarily focused on binary-valued decision problems, whereas the field of optimization has explored the broader spectrum of functions that are not limited to binary outputs. In this paper, we introduce and analyze the characteristics of valued decision problems in optimization settings. Specifically, we investigate the approximation properties of these problems in relation to their parametric decision counterparts. Our key contributions include proving that certain decision problems with parameterized definitions result in optimization problems that are limited to constant approximation, whereas other sporadically occurring decision problems allow for efficient constant approximation. Notably, our work addresses some longstanding open problems in the field. In this context, we examine the 1-way valued matching problem, the valued clique problem in graphs that lack certain edges, and problems involving extensions of graphs and orientations.

This study presents a novel numerical technique for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under constant diffusion, constant drift, and time-dependent potential. The method combines the Lagrange-Galerkin technique with a numerical solver for the resulting ODE. An alternative scheme is proposed when the method fails, and both approaches achieve first-order convergence globally and locally. The methods are applied to discrete mean field games, yielding optimal $N^{-1/2}$ error estimates. Numerical results support these findings.

Recent lepton flavor and charge universality violations in $b \to c$ decays hint at new physics beyond the Standard Model. This suggests that down-type b-quark decays involving a $c$-quark may be linked to leptoquark $U_1$, a color triplet that interacts with a charged electric force. As an effective field theory, $U_1$ can address the anomaly by resolving the conflict between $b \to c$ and $b \to u$. However, it predicts a highly suppressed rate for the $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ decay, in contradiction to experimental findings. This discrepancy arises from a mismatch in the relative magnitudes of couplings and form factors. A detailed study of this process within the $U_1$ leptoquark model takes into account both tree-level and one-loop level contributions.

The success of deep neural networks has surged in recent years, yet their robust performance comes as a mystery, given that traditional visualization techniques may fall short in explaining their decisions. This review delves into the current research on comprehending deep neural networks, addressing the challenges in explaining their decisions and the role of visualizations in facilitating the explanation of their performance. We categorize the studies that aim to comprehend deep neural networks based on the level of granularity they operate at, from the level of network components to the level of data samples, and the role of visualizations in explaining the performance of deep neural networks comes into question. We discuss the challenges associated with comprehending deep neural networks and the current limitations of visualizations in explaining their performance, and the research gaps that need to be addressed in the future.

Stars with extremely low temperatures and high rotation speeds in the FAP should theoretically possess exceptionally large radii due to centrifugal forces overcoming gravity. However, the observed radii of these stars are much smaller and close to their gravitational limits. Observations of high-rotation-speed stars in open clusters have revealed an unexpected correlation between radii and rotation speeds, with the fastest spinning examples showing the smallest radii. This discovery is counterintuitive and raises questions about the physical properties of these stars. Some researchers have proposed that the compact surfaces of rapidly rotating FAP stars may be the result of accretion/swallowed planets that transfer angular momentum to the star. While the existence of such objects cannot be ruled out, the evidence for this phenomenon remains inconclusive.

Multimodal news articles that integrate text and images are commonly consumed by the general public on social media platforms.  Unfortunately, false news stories frequently exploit this format to mislead viewers.  Given the harmful societal effects of spreading fake news, there is an urgent need for effective detection systems.  Although current multimodal false news detectors exist, they lack generalizability and require large amounts of labeled data for training.  To address these shortcomings, we propose an emergent multimodal false news detection framework based on the meta neural process network, allowing the model to learn from unseen datasets while incorporating prior multilabel classification knowledge.  Specifically, our meta-learning module is responsible for quickly adapting to new domains by leveraging available multimodal evidence, whereas the pre-trained classification network provides an initial estimate of the news authenticity.  For efficiency, a compact network is proposed to minimize inference time.  Comprehensive evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of our multimodal false news detection framework in terms of accuracy and efficiency, validating the efficacy of the meta-learning adaptation and efficient design multimodal evidence incorporation.

This research examines a cyclic transport equation, focusing on its mathematical properties. The study considers initial data and source terms with specific requirements. Cyclic transport equations can experience sudden changes or irregularities, known as singularities, at certain points. These singularities can spread and combine with the data defined by constants in directions opposite to the flow of the equation. Research has revealed that the equations maintain smoothness in two-dimensional planes when considering data that are not singular, but this changes in situations where singularities occur and is also affected by the relationship between the frequency of the cycle and integer values. This work extends existing concepts to include cyclic transport equations and explores their behavior in more complex, higher-dimensional scenarios.

This research investigates how certain factors influence a multi-server system's ability to provide up-to-date information in a status refreshing setup, where the age of information is a key performance indicator. Specifically, it examines using larger update sizes and efficiencies gained from having multiple servers to obtain more up-to-date information on each individual server. Unfortunately, earlier research failed to account for the potential negative impact of bigger update sizes and efficiency losses caused by multiple servers, as the widely used age of information metric does not easily express these factors. To address this limitation, it proposes the joint size and speed scale (JS^2) law, an approach that considers both server speed and update size to optimize system performance. The study also introduces a new performance indicator, average token age, to overcome the drawbacks of the traditional metric and provides theoretical and numerical results to validate the proposed JS^2 law and the introduced token age concept.

This work investigates various quantum group-like structures that arise from set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation, focusing on related properties such as quasi-bialgebras and their variations like weak and soft quasi-bialgebras. The paper provides new, comprehensive constructions of soft quasi-bialgebras and simplified proofs of previously obtained results, including modifications of tensor products of set-theoretic quantum groups and quantum double constructions. Additionally, it explores how certain set-theoretic solutions can yield soft quasi-bialgebras that are not isomorphic to any quantum group-like structure.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices and pairs of complementary matrices have been translated to the domain of arrays by multiple researchers. These Complementary Multi-Dimensional Arrays (CMDA) are useful in various applications such as multi-user detection in Code Division Multiple Access systems and Direction of Arrival estimation in Multiple Input Multiple Output radar technology. In this research, extensions of the Golay complementary arrays concept are made into complex-valued and multi-dimensional forms. New construction techniques for CMDCAs are proposed using complementary matrices, Golay sequences, and Chu sequences. Specifically, four construction methods are introduced, and associated complementary structures are the Hadamard gates, phase rotations of unity, and zeros.

Recent experiments in silicon have revealed a unique phenomenon called valley interference, which arises due to the coupling of electrons with the crystal lattice. In order to better understand this effect, researchers used scanning tunneling microscopy to observe direct evidence of spin-swapping in silicon, where the d-wave symmetry of the resonant states was found to be caused by intervalley coupling and real-space spin-swapping in a single-atom SiSiSiSi tetramer. This line of inquiry has led to the observation of unique magnetic anisotropy and valley-swapping in a bi-tetramer when subjected to an applied electric field, which also resulted in a lineshape that was consistent with a lineshape derived from a minimal four-valley model.

Graph neural networks are a cutting-edge area of research with a range of applications, and this paper provides a cutting-edge overview of their most recent development. It specifically targets their most difficult aspect: temporal and dynamic graph learning. We've broken down complex systems into simpler components, exploring various approaches to their structure and a specific set of methods for their temporal and dynamic aspects. Additionally, we've identified key research areas for future development in this field.

We introduce two novel concepts in the study of integer partitions, specifically weak-dominance and 3-exchange dominance, which possess the 2-coskeletal property. This characteristic allows application in homotopy theory to endow these relations with homotopy equivalence. Conversely, in non-Abelian settings, relations acquire homotopy equivalence, providing a basis for Green's conjecture on the stable homotopy groups.

This study introduces an original framework called Bipolar Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (BPAVE) to create artificial brain injury images from normal ones. Initially, we adapted the BPAVE model by integrating two separate discriminator networks at opposite encoder levels into the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) architecture. Next, we modified it to gradually introduce errors during the image generation process. Comparing BPAVE to other methods on the open-access OASIS dataset demonstrated its superiority in terms of Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM).

The study of quantum correlations in mixed qudit states from an unextendible product basis presents a challenge due to the inclusion of noisy states in product bases that admit separable PPT decompositions. As an alternative, we investigate nonlocality robustness in an 'X-state', consisting of the reverse of an UPB with two extendable product states of qudits odd dimension greater than three. Nonlocality robustness values are calculated for various odd dimensional Grover and Bell UPBs, along with unitary-transformed versions, and unitary-extended versions. Our findings indicate that nonlocality robustness values are consistent across different unitary-transformed UPBs and unitary-extended UPBs, providing valuable nonlocality non-robustness insights for these units-related UPBs. Moreover, we establish an upper limit for nonlocality robustness in unit-related UPBs and observe that the limit is achieved when the unit-related UPBs have the lowest odd dimension, specifically five.

In the fifth iteration of the astrobot technology, complete safe coordination across the entire telescope floor has been achieved. This advancement enables the entire SDSS-V survey to be effectively completed. The implementation of the astrobot system has been successfully tested on the BOSS deck at the Apache Point Observatory, where data from monitoring sensors and sensor coordination algorithms have been collected and analyzed to ensure the reliability and effectiveness of the system.

The standard GP 2 compiler is a highly versatile tool suitable for both research and practical applications. Its versatility is due to the compiler's ability to leverage an existing abstract syntax tree, which was originally created for the GRI language. This feature allows GP 2 to rapidly integrate new and experimental language constructs by reusing the abstract syntax tree. However, incorporating object-oriented programming concepts required significant modifications to the parser and symbol table. These changes made it difficult to incorporate such concepts in a library-based approach. In contrast, the new enhanced compiler introduces a new parser that preserves backward compatibility with the GRI language while enabling the inclusion of additional grammars. As a result, a new, intuitive object-oriented programming language called GRI++ has been created and is now available for use in the GRI platform.

To address the lack of a universally applicable method for retrieving and organizing information from social media platforms, a novel approach is proposed. This approach focuses on creating a unified structure to extract key information, including text, images, videos, and metadata, using a self-supervised learning technique called contrastive learning. By leveraging a large amount of unannotated data, this method learns to represent and extract a wide range of content without the need for extensive labeling. The proposed framework consists of three main components: a unified structure for feature extraction, a set of extraction operators, and a retraining module. By building upon the contrastive learning step, the model can effectively use the features it has learned to link posts to their corresponding accounts and maintain a database of user information. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in accurately retrieving and making sense of content from social media platforms.

Wreath and twisted wreath type graphs have been recognized as infinitely numerous distinct groups. Recently, researchers investigated their relationship with semi-normal and star normal quotients, focusing specifically on twisted wreath type groups. This study presents the first collections of groups that satisfy the criteria for star normality, equivalence to the classes of twisted wreath type and SC-groups, and provides an infinite quantity of groups that meet these conditions.

Working with categorical data in machine learning and statistics is complicated due to the need to identify parameters for each variable level. When dealing with many such variables, it is common to combine them with a penalty that considers the group of binary variables. This paper introduces an improvement to the Group Lasso penalty that encourages sparsity at the variable level, resulting in more interpretable and effective models. We also propose an efficient algorithm to execute this modified penalty and demonstrate its superiority over the original Group Lasso through both synthetic and real-world data tests.

Large language models have recently achieved remarkable success, yet their
inability to seamlessly integrate structured human-made knowledge presents a
significant limitation. We introduce a novel approach called SKILL, which
utilizes a structured knowledge module as an additional language model's
component. This module serves as a virtual expert that provides real-time
answers to queries within predefined boundaries. By employing a attention
mechanism, the model can selectively inject structured knowledge when required,
otherwise it relies solely on its existing capabilities. Experimental results
demonstrate that SKILL allows for seamless integration of various knowledge
formats such as graphs, formulas, and tables, while also outperforming
traditional integration methods both with and without pre-training on existing
datasets.

This article examines various nonlocal diffusion models and their associated convergent approximations, both directly and via limiting processes like Gamma-convergence.  In doing so, it scrutinizes the mathematical structures underlying these models and their generated solutions, with a view towards establishing a structural consistency across them.  With this perspective, the article also introduces and analyses new models that incorporate influence functions with quadratic scaling, which are shown to have parabolic PDE descriptions with nondivergence type operators.  The article demonstrates the direct convergence of these models to local solutions while exploring the outcomes of changing the domain size parameter after optimal scaling.  Furthermore, the article investigates a broader class of discontinuous influence functions within the kernel class, resulting in the identification of Besov-type equations in their optimal settings.  With regard to suboptimal cases, the article establishes the introduction of effective kernels with the associated direct solutions, nonlocal diffusion operators, and the corresponding local diffusion operators.

This research on panoramic stitching stitching focuses on minimal assumptions, specifically excluding the need to assume a scene that adheres to a specific geometric pattern. Instead, it prioritizes solving the problem under what is known as "gravity prior," which states that objects in the scene generally align with the direction of gravity. The researcher demonstrates that, under this prior, it is feasible to determine the relative orientation of the camera's views, provided that at least one object in the scene is present. Building on this, it is also possible to solve for the relative scale and orientation of the camera's views, provided that the objects in the scene are of a consistent size. These findings are then applied to the creation of seamless panoramic images from images that were taken from varying angles, provided that certain conditions are met, specifically that the images were not taken lying completely on their sides and that there is enough overlap between the images and that they share at least one object. The outcome of this research is a robust algorithm for creating high-quality panoramic images that are free from unnecessary distortions.

This article outlines the key steps in proving that certain Eisenstein series, associated with $GL(n)$ and having an arbitrary central character, can be expressed using linear combinations of non-related Eisenstein series, each with a distinct central character.

This study examines the decline in motor activity in Parkinson's disease, a neurological disorder, and its underlying mechanisms. A novel biophysical model is proposed to simulate the Parkinson's-damaged basal ganglia by incorporating the interactions of neurons within specific brain circuits. A key objective is to replicate the reduced motor activity by simulating the impaired globus pallidus exterus output. We achieved this by first implementing a healthy model, which accurately represented normal neuronal activity, before introducing specific disruptions to model the effects of Parkinson's disease on dopamine neurons. Subsequently, the model's parameters were adjusted using an optimization method and data derived from electrical recordings of the brains of common marmoset monkeys. The resulting Parkinson's model demonstrated a variety of abnormal electrical activity patterns, oscillations, and circuit behaviors, which aligned with observed motor activity deficits. Moreover, the model's predictions regarding the connectivity between distinct brain areas were shown to be consistent with the motor activity deficits observed in Parkinson's disease.

This paper introduces a novel anti-aliasing technique for line join kernels in HTML5 Canvas and WebGL, enabling high-quality vector map rendering at various scales using OpenStreetMap data. Unlike existing methods, our anti-aliasing approach is computationally efficient, allowing for real-time animation and rendering of up to ten thousand path elements in HTML5 Canvas and WebGL. Our technique has been implemented in multiple open-source open map applications and is available for use through npm packages.

Our research centers on nine extremely luminous galaxies, located less than 0.04 units of distance from Earth, observed through the KOOLS-IFU on the Seimei Telescope. These galaxies, categorized as ultraluminous or luminous infrared galaxies, often show signs of merging and have optical spectra that reveal a high infrared luminosity. Through spectral analysis, we found these galaxies to be predominantly surface bright with very little gas present. Their star formation rates are exceptionally high, typically associated with the merging process. Notably, we identified significant substructures in their spectra that could indicate the presence of distinct galaxy populations.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, non-linear minimum function that calculates the straight-line distance between two points in multidimensional space. This function is based on a transcendental expression. By integrating this function into RBF-based interpolation, we obtain a non-linear minimum function radial basis function. Theoretical analysis shows that this QI operator can achieve convergence at a rate of O(h^2) for any piecewise continuous function. Numerical experiments confirm that the QI operator based on the new function can accurately reproduce complex curves and surfaces, including those with sharp angles, with a low error rate of approximately 10^-3.

Accurate weather categorization is crucial for public safety, as well as for the stability of transportation, the agriculture industry, and outdoor events.  Deep learning techniques have shown great promise in solving complex image classification problems, yet their practical application to weather forecasting remains underdeveloped due to the scarcity of comprehensive, multi-category weather datasets.  To address this issue, we introduce the first publicly available dataset that encompasses a diverse range of weather conditions, including the basics of the 101-type cloud classification system.  Examinations of various Convolutional Neural Network architectures, from the ResNet family to the MobileNet series, were conducted on this dataset to identify the most effective configurations for accurate weather forecasting.  To overcome limitations associated with the relatively small size of our dataset, we also explored the use of data augmentation as a means of enhancing classification performance.  As part of this study, a range of data augmentation strategies were tested to optimize the results.  Our findings demonstrate that the best possible accuracy of 98.8% can be attained through a combination of the ResNet101 architecture and a specific set of data augmentation techniques.

Multi-channel audio capture can suffer from background noise that degrades listening and analysis quality, but is essential for natural, noise-free audio and effective speech processing. This project explores a novel single-channel noise reduction model called DPCRN, which combines an acoustic noise record with real-time processing to create a noise-free audio output. The model draws on past audio recordings as training data, a unique approach not limited by the need for clean reference audio. By training on noisy samples with corresponding clean components, the model learns to supplement the single-channel noisy audio with a clear noise signal for improved quality. The model's dual-path convolution recurrent network architecture is well-suited to this unconventional learning paradigm. Experimental results on the Aishalman audio dataset show the model's ability to significantly enhance audio clarity, outperforming existing single-channel enhancement methods.

A relativistic $f(R)$ gravity theory is examined in the context of cosmology and the formation of structures, particularly how it influences dark matter halo properties at their turn-around stage. Researchers have used a modified field equation from the $f(R)$ gravity theory, adopting a Dvali-Gabadadze-Porrati (DGP) branch, to simulate the expansion of the universe and calculate its impact on dark matter halo properties. Through a "fitting length" parameter, they were able to fit the universe's expansion equation and obtain a Milne universe for a specific choice of this parameter. In this study, a $\frac{m_{\nu}^2}{m_{\rm Pl}^2} \phi_{,R}$ term is added to the action of the $f(R)$ gravity, allowing for a simulation of the universe's expansion that incorporates both extra scalar degrees of freedom and the effects of neutrino masses. As a result, this modified simulation was able to accurately predict turn-around radii for a diverse range of halo masses over an extended period, while maintaining a fit to the Hubble parameter and the dimensionless function f$\sigma_8$.

This study aims to develop a multi-fluid model for simulating Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, which can contribute to understanding atmospheric convection.  At the heart of this study lies the development of a two-fluid model for Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, constrained by fixed temperatures and fixed flux conditions, and characterized by differing thermal conductivities and viscosities for the two fluids. A key feature of Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection is the presence of oscillatory patterns, and thus, it is imperative that the multi-fluid model accurately captures these dynamics. Consequently, careful consideration must be given to the numerical algorithms and the grid arrangement of the fluid layers to prevent spurious oscillations arising from thermal discontinuities.  When implementing a two-fluid model based on non-oscillatory numerical algorithms, distinct oscillatory patterns emerge that persist over an extended period.  However, by adopting an arrangement in which the fluid with the lower Rayleigh number resides at the heated base, the oscillations are significantly dampened, and in certain instances, they are virtually eliminated.  This outcome underscores the potential for bias in numerical convection simulations when employing multi-fluid approaches, a phenomenon that has potential implications for observations made using atmospheric lidar systems.

We analyze a system of two independently correlated quantum harmonic oscillators that have been randomly entangled with two separate quantum atoms, each interacting with their respective oscillators under the Jaynes-Teller framework. By examining the changes in the atoms' correlations over time, we investigate how the initial uncertainty and the inherent connection between the atoms influence one another. Our research reveals that the unknown nature of the harmonic oscillator parameters can actually contribute to maintaining long-term entanglement in the quantum atoms, while a certain level of initial uncertainty in the bosonic systems can impede the development of entanglement, and be directly related to an excess of correlations in the atoms. Notably, increasing the interaction strength between the atoms and the harmonic systems leads to more significant differences in the expected values of observables, and a decrease in prior uncertainty in the bosonic systems can actually result in reduced entrapment of the atoms due to excessive correlations induced.

The CMS Experiment at the LHC in Geneva has been upgraded to examine Upgrade 1 and beyond Upgrade 1 scenarios. As part of this upgrade, the interaction region has been enhanced with additional detectors including silicon strip and twin calorimeters, alongside new pixel detectors and modules. A particular focus has been given to analyzing the reconstruction of novel components, specifically the pixel pilot blades. This examination involved re-running 2016 data utilizing upgraded reconstruction algorithms, and comparing the results to traditional methods. Furthermore, it also included an examination of data obtained from 2018 beam tests utilizing the production of J/$\psi$ mesons via decaying muons. These assessments demonstrated successful pilot blade reconstruction in both instances, and as a result, they are set to be incorporated into future interactions.

Lattice QCD is a suitable approach for studying the ground state properties of the SU(2) gluonium, particularly its constituent quark-antiquark scattering states and the associated coupled-channel dynamics. Initial investigations into the scalar SU(2) meson spectrum from quark-antiquark pairs and gluonic components using the Euclidean time correlation matrix have shown significant progress. Notably, a Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral representation fit has been achieved for the su(2) gluonium channel at the scale of 2.44(6) GeV, with further analysis of the residue demonstrating the presence of excited states in the spectrum.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations to track the public's emotions towards products, services, and
various topics. While the public's feedback can be both beneficial and detrimental,
understanding the prevailing sentiment becomes crucial. This paper outlines a
sentiment analysis system that leverages Long Short-Term Memory networks and achieves
an accuracy of 0.85 on a benchmark dataset.

A linear screening compositeness principle was previously established for
  certain charged black holes in anti-de Sitter space with non-zero mass, and
  we investigate whether this principle holds for black holes with a non-linear
  photon field, and find that it indeed does.  We obtain a non-linear version of
  the charge principle from and near the event horizon of these black holes,
  demonstrating its validity throughout the near-horizon region, and verify that
  it aligns with the standard charged Reissner–Nordström black holes.  However,
  shade caloricity cannot be achieved in this context.  Furthermore, we explore
  the relationship between the photon field and the charged black hole's horizon,
  and observe that a certain type of photon field contributes to a decrease in
  the horizon's charge capacity.

Reconstructing a quantum state using a method called quantum tomography is hindered by the complexity of the state, which can be alleviated through an alternative approach. This method involves operating on the statistical data obtained from the tomographic representation, specifically tailored for coherent states of the parabolic Anderson equation with random obstacles. Two specific transformations are examined in this context: entanglement changes induced by a unitary operation and the onset of synchronization resulting from the application of a periodic drive. These phenomena are studied in both classical and quantum systems, with the success of quantum synchronization directly linked to the level of entanglement present.

Building a dialogue system that adheres to a particular role is a particularly challenging problem.  To address this problem, a novel data annotation approach is presented that effectively captures the specified role through four key aspects: a role description, the dialogue history, an emotional state, and a set of role-specific constraints.  These requirements are essential in ensuring the dialogue system's performance in emulating the designated role.  A prototype implementation of the role-specific dialogue system is developed and its capabilities are demonstrated through a user study that shows users' preference for the role-specification over basic data-driven responses.  Furthermore, the role-specification approach is further refined by optimizing the model's ability to adhere to the four key aspects of the role.  The role-specification approach is also evaluated on a larger dataset comprising 2400 utterances and the results show that the system's performance is significantly improved.  The role-specification approach is also shown to be scalable and can be applied to larger datasets.  The role-specification approach is found to be particularly effective in emulating complex roles and the results are consistent with the role's intended behavior.  The role-specification approach is also found to be particularly useful in scenarios where the data is limited or the role is highly nuanced.  The role-specification approach is found to be particularly effective in emulating a wide range of roles and the results are consistent with the role's intended behavior.  The role-specification approach is also found to be particularly useful

Choosing effective agricultural practices is crucial due to the complex nature of farming systems and the multitude of available options. When farmers aim to optimize yields and minimize costs, pesticide usage can seem like an obvious solution. Nevertheless, the environmental and public health implications of pesticide use have prompted the exploration of more sustainable alternatives. As the agricultural sector shifts away from pesticide dependence, the need to carefully evaluate the performance of various management approaches has grown. However, the assessment of agricultural practices is often hindered by noisy performance data, making it challenging to accurately compare the effects of different methods.
